She turns and walks on. After three steps she speaks without looking back.

"The dead-house is Fist property. You come in as my witness. You don't touch anything I don't hand you, and your name goes in my book along with the hour. If any of that doesn't suit you, the lanes are uphill."

The cat comes back to James's heel without being called twice. It walks pressed close to his boot, and through the link he gets the quay behind them from a foot off the ground: dark gaps between the warehouses, a bollard, black water slapping the stones. Nothing moves that shouldn't.

The dead-house turns out to be a squat stone shed in the lee of the Seatower causeway, with a lamp burning in a barred window. Inside it smells of quicklime and brine, and of the cold that never quite leaves stone near water. There are three slabs and all of them are empty. An old Fist man with one sleeve pinned up sits dozing on a stool by the brazier. He opens an eye, sees Brask, and closes it again.

"Hobb went to the paupers' ground Thursday," Brask says, mostly to herself. "Nobody claimed him. His things stay until someone does."

She takes a pine box down from a shelf of pine boxes, each one chalked with a name, and sets it on the nearest slab. Before she opens it she takes a small oilcloth-bound book from inside her tabard, writes a line in it, and turns it away from James while she writes. Then the book goes back where it came from and the lid comes off.

There is a pair of porter's boots, cracked across the toes and stiff with dried salt. Beside them, on a twist of sacking, lies the copper.

James sees at once that it isn't any coin of the Gate. It's too thin and too old, and both faces have been worn down almost smooth, the way a coin wears after years in a pocket or a fist. In the lamplight one face still holds the ghost of a woman's head, tilted a little, and she's smiling. The other face shows nothing at all.

At James's feet the cat has gone stiff. Through the link comes the same smell again, strong this time and fresh from the box: copper that has sat in a hand until it smells of the hand, and under it the cold salt of deep water.

James has spent enough years in southern ports to know how sailors pay Umberlee. They throw her due over the rail before a voyage, or into a storm when the storm is already on them, and they throw it into the sea. In all those years he never saw anyone put a coin between a drowned man's teeth.

Brask leaves the copper on its sacking and doesn't hand it to him. She stands back with her arms folded and watches him look at it.

"You're the Lady's man," she says. "Does that look like an offering to Umberlee to you?"

His coin smells of him: leather, road sweat, the Saltwind's tar, and copper warmed by his own skin. It's familiar, a smell the cat would follow through any crowd. Of the two coins, only that one carries it. The cat pulls back from it and sits pressed against his shin.

Brask puts the lantern down. For a moment she looks at the door, then at the keeper, who hasn't moved. Then she takes the oilcloth book from inside her tabard again. This time she doesn't turn it away. She opens it to a page near the back, lays it flat on the slab beside the two coins, and puts her finger under the first line.

The handwriting is small, square and Fist-taught. There are seven names, each with a date, and next to each name a few words that have nothing to do with the sea.

*Wenna Tull, net-mender. Hauled up a purse in her net, 12 gp.*
*Orrin Vasse, carter. Dray overturned on Stonyhill, walked out from under it.*
*Halder Cobb, dicer. Won big, guest table.* In the margin, underlined twice: *the Wheel.*
*Tam Rook, deckhand. Aunt in Scornubel died, left him a house.*
*Sefton Marr, clerk. Debts paid off in one night.* In the margin: *the Wheel.*
*Nell, no other name. Survived the fever ward at Twin Songs.*
*Garret Hobb, porter. Three hands running at Malloway's crate.*

Every one of them was pulled out of the harbour, and every one had a copper in the mouth.

"Seven since the thaw," Brask says. "Filed as sea business, all seven. I asked one of Umberlee's women about the coins. She spat on the floor of the Fist hall, and I had to mop it." It comes out as flat as everything else she says. "You said receipt. You're the first person besides me to say it out loud."

She leaves the book open on the slab, but her hand stays flat beside it.

"The Wheel's a gaming house behind the inner wall. Patriar money, invitation only. The Watch's ground, not ours. I can't walk in there in this tabard." Her eyes go to his coin, then to his face. "So it's my turn, Worgen. Every name on that page had a stroke of luck in the month before the water took them."

She looks at him the same way she looked at him over the lantern on the quay.

"You crossed the sea to the Gate on the Lady's errand. Have you been lucky lately?"

She doesn't interrupt. When he gets to *about due for the harbour*, she turns the oilcloth book back toward herself, finds the first blank line under Garret Hobb, and writes. "So I know where to start," she says, "if it's you."

She lets *a house collecting* go by without a word, but she looks at the turned head on the copper again when he says it. When he offers to go where her tabard can't, she gives a short breath through her nose and says nothing at all for a moment. On his stool the keeper shifts and goes on snoring.

There's no ledge outside, just a lip of crumbling mortar two fingers wide that wouldn't hold a pigeon. Somewhere toward the middle of the night a Fist patrol goes by with two lanterns, and boots ring and fade. A drunk stops under the corner lamp to argue with it and moves on. What he gets through the link comes from a foot off the ground, then from no ground at all. The cat crosses the quay under a cart, between the wheels, and slips through the doorway into the shadow.

Inside, the salt-house is huge and dim. It's one long hall with light coming in thin through the gaps in the boards. The beams overhead are furred white with old salt, and long pale ghosts on the floor show where salt piles stood for decades. It smells of dry rot, gull droppings and rats. Under all of that is the ordinary harbour salt that every building on this quay soaks up.

The inner door is at the far end, a plank door in a plank partition. It's shut. The cat doesn't try it. It goes up a post with its claws, along a beam, and James feels the jump in his own stomach. The partition stops two feet short of the roof, and the cat drops over the top into the dark beyond.

This is where the smell changes.

The room behind the partition has no floor, only a broad stone stair going down into black water. It's an old water-gate, built so salt barges could be unloaded straight from the harbour under cover. The iron grille over the arch at the bottom is rusted half up, and the tide slaps through the gap. A flat little skiff is tied to a ring on the lowest dry step, with a wet coil of rope in it. On a peg by the stair hangs a grey wool cloak, dark at the hem where it's been dipped in the sea and left to dry over and over.

Down here the deep salt is everywhere: the clean, cold salt of deep water, so thick the cat's whiskers go flat. The cat goes down the stair one step at a time, nose to the stone, trying to sort out where it's strongest.

The cat doesn't find where it's strongest. Down by the water the deep salt isn't in any one spot. It's in the stone, the rope, the cloak, the skiff and the sea itself, and it's so thick that the cat's nose stops sorting and just takes it all in. It puts its nose to the cloak and gets deep salt. It tries the skiff's gunwale and gets deep salt. It tries the wet edge of the lowest step and gets the same again. It can't tell whether the grey man's own smell is in any of it, or whether it all comes from the black water coming in under the grille. The cat sneezes, then sneezes again. Its whiskers stay flat against its face, and it backs up two steps as if the water had moved toward it, though it hasn't.

So it answers the question it can. The inner door doesn't lead anywhere in the city. It leads to the harbour, to a hidden stair, a boat, and a grey cloak that keeps getting wet.

Then, because James told it to be quick, it goes. It goes up the stair, up the post and over the partition in one long jump, along the beam and down. It crosses the great pale hall at a run and comes out of the doorway into the sun so fast the gull on the lintel lifts off squawking.

James opens his eyes. The small beer is warm in his hand, the porters are still shouting at the ship on the tide, and nobody on the bench or at the hatch is looking at him. A moment later the cat comes out from under a cart and sits against his boot. It washes its face hard with both paws, as if it could scrub the smell out of its nose, and doesn't stop for a long time.

Over the water, the Seatower's bell strikes the quarter after ten.

I don't turn around. I keep my eyes on her face and my arms folded, like a man still haggling over terms.

"Before I pick, there's something you should know. Don't look." I keep my voice flat. "While I was talking, the cat caught him again, on the breeze off the water. It wasn't coming from the crowd. It came from that row of tarred lighters under canvas, about forty paces up past the barge queue. It was fresh, from this hour. Then the wind came round off the river and lost it. The cat didn't see anyone. But somebody in one of those boats is close enough to watch us talk."

I unfold my arms and nod toward the table, as if we've settled some ordinary business.

"So: Kettle's tonight, steps tomorrow at low water, with you and the muffled boat. If he's watching me, I want him watching me in a dice cellar with a drink, not hanging round your steps two nights running. Tomorrow's ebb comes an hour later, near enough. That's still dark, and still big."

Then, lower still:

"Ask Haskel to listen for more than oars tonight. If one of those lighters slips its line after the lamps, I want to know which one, and which way it goes." I touch two fingers to my brow, lazy, for whoever's watching. "I'll leave word with him before the bells at two if I'm still breathing. If I'm not, page eight."

I turn and walk off up Cable Lane at an easy pace, the long way round, away from the lighters.

Through the link, to the cat: *Don't look at the boats. Walk with me. If that smell follows us off the quay, tell me which side it's on.*

Brask doesn't look. Her eyes stay on his face. When he says *lighters*, the only movement is her thumb, which stops on the edge of the oilcloth book under her tabard and stays there.

"Forty paces," she says, to him and not to the water. "The tarred ones under canvas are salt-lighters. They've been laid up since before the thaw." She lets that sit for a moment. "Every boat on this harbour pays the harbourmaster mooring by the month, and his book says who pays. His book is Fist ground." That's all she says about it. Whatever she means to do with the book, she plans to do it when nobody is watching her do it.

When he picks Kettle's tonight and the steps tomorrow, she nods once.

"Tomorrow. Low water's nearer the second bell. Come to the dead-house an hour before and knock twice. Haskel won't open for one." Her eyes flick to his brow as the lazy salute comes up, then back. "He'll hear a line slip. He hears a rat change its mind."

She turns half toward the trestle table and lifts her voice to the flat, carrying pitch she uses for the queue.

"Next."

Anyone watching from the water sees a sellsword who asked about Fist work and got turned away.

I go on up Cable Lane to the blue door without stopping anywhere else.

If Tansy is about, I put two silver on the newel post where she'll see them. "Lamplighting came early. Remembered, not accounted."

Up in the top room I check the shutter first: is the scrap of card still wedged low between frame and sill, where I left it? Then the mattress, head and foot, for both bags, and the shadow behind the washbasin for the crossbow. If anything has moved, I want to know before I do anything else.

If it's all as I left it, I sit on the bed, take my papers out of the pack and spread them on the three-legged table, next to where the card case sat this morning. I've carried two of them since the south without really looking at them. The night I won, the promissory note was just money, and I put the letter from my old company away half-read because I didn't want what was in it. Now I'm in the city the Lady sent me to, a man has been watching me from a boat, and every name in Brask's book had a run of luck before the water took him.

So I read the promissory note properly this time: who signed it, for how much, drawn on whom, and payable where. Then I open the letter and read it to the end.

The cat can have the sill and the sun. *Watch the lane. I'm busy for a bit.*

When I'm done, I'll lie down for a couple of hours with my boots by the bed. Kettle's runs until two, low water's after that, and I want to be awake for both.

The blue door is on the latch at this hour. Inside, Tansy sits at the kitchen table with a colander between her knees, shelling peas. She doesn't look up when the stairs creak under his boot. She looks up when two silver pieces click down on the newel post.

"Lamplighting came early," James says. "Remembered, not accounted."

Tansy looks at the coins and then out the window at the full daylight in the yard. "Lamplighting is when the lamps are lit. It isn't whenever a lodger gets bored." A pea pod snaps. She gets down off the stool anyway, walks to the post, picks up both coins and turns each one over before they go into her apron. "There. Now I've forgotten them." She goes back to the peas. "Don't track tar up my stairs."

The top room is warm under the roof, and it smells of hot slate and lavender.

He checks the shutter first. The folded card is still wedged low between the frame and the sill, at the same angle and the same depth, with the crease facing the room where he left it. He runs his hand under the head of the mattress and finds one bag, then under the foot and finds the other. Both are tied with the Counting House knot and neither looks lighter. Behind the washbasin the crossbow lies in the shadow of the pitch-mended crack with the bolts beside it, exactly as he put them down. Nobody has been in.

The cat jumps to the sill when he tells it to, folds itself into the strip of sun there and turns its ears toward the lane. Through the link come the ropewalk's hemp dust, the noon smell of frying onions from next door and a cart going downhill. It notices nothing it hasn't already sorted.

James sits on the bed and takes his papers out of the pack.

---

The promissory note is heavy paper, folded in three, and softer at the creases than it was a month ago. He opens it flat on the three-legged table and reads it properly for the first time.

The hand is careful and very young. Every letter is joined the way a tutor teaches it.

*On presentation, the Counting House of Baldur's Gate shall pay to the bearer three hundred gold pieces from the account of the House of Ammerstead. Given in good faith at the table, on the night written below.*

It is signed *Aurel Ammerstead*, with a flourish under the surname that wobbles at the end.

James holds the paper up to the light from the crack in the shutter. There is a watermark in the sheet, faint as breath: a shield, and on it a salt-cellar. Tansy laughed about those arms this morning. Nobody's allowed to laugh at them.

He remembers the hand that wrote this. It was soft and pale, with ink on the second finger and no calluses anywhere. A fair-haired young man of twenty or so sat across from him in that card room in the south. He gave only his first name and bet like someone who had never needed to count. On the last hand he pushed his stake in before he'd properly looked at his cards. At the time James had been busy praying and took it for nerves. Looking back with a gambler's eye, it doesn't sit right. The young man hadn't looked nervous. He'd looked like someone getting a thing over with. When he lost, he smiled and asked for paper.

James turns the note over. In the bottom corner of the back, in pencil and half smudged by a month in the pack, is a quick sketch: a woman's face, laughing with her head thrown back, and a coin held up between two of her fingers. It's only a few lines, the kind of thing a bored man draws while someone else is shuffling. He didn't notice it that night.

---

The letter is thinner, cheap paper, sealed once with a lump of candle wax that he broke a month ago and pressed shut again with his thumb. Halfway down the first side is the place where he stopped reading.

He reads it from the beginning.

*Jem,*

*Orso says you've left us for good this time. I'm not writing to call you back by the ear. You know where the company winters, and your place stays open until midsummer whether you come or not.*

*I'm writing because none of us said it to your face, and somebody should. We all saw where it was going. Every one of us watched you at those tables and kept quiet, because you're good company and you always paid your share in the end. That was cowardice on our part. I buried a man last winter for the dice, and I won't stand by the grave of a second one and say I didn't know.*

That's where he stopped a month ago. He keeps going.

*If you ever get out of the south, Wil Harrow, who carried the colours at Darromar, took the Flaming Fist's coin in Baldur's Gate. The last I heard he was a quartermaster at Wyrm's Rock. He'd stand you a drink. He wouldn't stand you a stake, so maybe that's the man to find.*

*Keep your head down and your hands where people can see them.*

*Ysolde.*

There's nothing else on it, not even a postscript.

---

He lays the two papers side by side on the table, where the card case sat this morning. Then he lies down on the lavender mattress with his boots by the bed and the rapier against the frame.

Sleep comes easier than he expected. The link carries the afternoon into it in small pieces: the ropewalk men calling the lengths, a barrow wheel that needs grease, Tansy's broom on the front step. At one point the half-eared tom comes along the ropewalk roof, sees who has the sill and sits down twelve feet below to wash, keeping his back to the window to show he hasn't noticed. Nobody stops under the window. There's no deep salt, no smoke and no wax.

When James opens his eyes, the strip of sun has moved off the sill and onto the wall above the washbasin, and it has gone the colour of late afternoon. Somewhere toward the market the bells are finishing a quarter past three. The cat is still at its post. When it feels him wake, it sends a single image of the tom's back with an opinion behind it.

The note and the letter lie where he left them.

## Player's note: Session 1, "Envoy of Luck"

### What worked

**The people.** Brask is the best NPC I've met in an AI-run game. She has a flat voice, an arm's-length habit, writes everything in the book, says "Next." and "page eight", and never once warms up in a way that feels unearned. Tansy, Patience, Pip and the alewife each felt like a separate person with their own reason to talk or not talk, not a quest dispenser. Patience's "I didn't have what they were looking for" was exactly the kind of careful answer I wanted to chew on.

**The cat as an instrument.** Smell as the cat's sense, with a consistent palette, carried the whole investigation:
- *deep salt / wet wool / lamp-black* for the grey man
- *censer smoke / wax* for the Wheel
- *hand-warmed copper* for the coins

When the cat found the scent on the Kettle's rail and then on the breeze from the lighters, it felt like evidence, not GM fiat. The cat's failures also stayed honest: the water-gate was too saturated to read.

**Continuity and bookkeeping.** These were all tracked without my asking:
- lent items (the needle, Marr's marker) and debts ("remembered, not accounted")
- the card under the shutter
- the copper in the crack being gone by morning

The state felt trustworthy.

**Failures that still moved things.** Missed Perception rolls gave me partial pictures and a clear "here's what it would take to learn more", never a dead end. The low-tide plan came directly out of a failed roll. That's good design.

**The promissory note.** Aurel Ammerstead signing my winnings, the salt-cellar watermark, the laughing-woman sketch, the realization that he *wanted* to lose: that's the hook landing, and it recontextualized everything from day one. The turned head on the drowned men's coppers against the facing head on mine is a lovely visual clue.

**Asking about the letter.** Flagging that it wasn't on my record, and inventing it in a way that adds Wil Harrow as a possible crew contact, was the right call.

### What broke

**The roll cards used the wrong modifiers. This is the big one.**

| Check | Sheet value | Card added | Totals |
|---|---|---|---|
| Persuasion | +7 | +4 | 21 should be 24 |
| Deception | +7 | +4 | 16 should be 19 |
| Perception | +1 | +2 | Card label even reads "+2 Perception +1" |

It looks like the server is passing the bare ability modifier and dropping proficiency. No outcome flipped this session, but on a 13 it would have, and I'd have had no idea why. Please check how `skill` resolves.

**Healing Light dice cap mismatch.** The sheet says up to 5 dice at once; the records panel says 4.

**Retroactive summary paragraphs.** Paragraphs like "Looking back, James knows the lie worked…" sometimes appeared after the out-of-game note. They repeat what the narration already showed, in a slightly odd retrospective voice.

**Over-long out-of-game notes.** The four-item explanation of why nothing needed a roll read like the GM defending itself to an auditor rather than talking to me. One line is enough.

### What was missing (or what I'm watching)

**The heist premise hasn't surfaced yet.** That's fine on day two, and I understand "believe the simple version first". But two in-game days were pure legwork, and the drowned-men mystery is so compelling it could quietly become the whole campaign. I'd like a nudge soon toward:
- *what Tymora wants brought back*
- *crew*

Brask, Patience, Pip and Wil Harrow all smell like candidates. I'd love the first "price, interest, secret" conversation in the next session or two.

**No temptation yet.** Pip's free turn was a nice first touch, but the cards haven't really been leaned on. Kettle's tonight is the obvious place.

**Pacing.** Pacing was patient, maybe a hair slow. A short time-skip offer would have helped, something like "nothing else happens before the lamps unless you want it to."

Overall: a strong opening. It's grounded, consistent, and the world felt like it was running without me. Fix the roll modifiers and I'm very happy.

Every signal said *this one matters* and nothing said *don't*. I held off because the goddess's ban is the one rule James has, and breaking it in a rented room with nobody watching felt like cheating the premise before the campaign had earned it. But if the GM had put one more small pressure on — Mirela at the door, say, or the chandler's stamp turning out to be a wheel — I think James turns it, and I'd have let him. I'm not sure I was right to wait. A weakness you never test isn't a weakness.

The other was smaller. When the singer finished and the dust started drifting again, I wanted to send Copper up into the rafters. Not me with a lantern — him, silent, to sit on that beam and see what a cat sees when there's no one there. I'd just promised Bram I wouldn't climb his beams, and it felt like the kind of promise a man like James keeps to the letter and breaks in spirit, which is exactly the move I didn't want to make on the first night with a goddess watching. So I didn't. But the cat flattened his fur like he'd been *recognised*, and I walked away from that. I'll be thinking about it until the next session.

And a half-one: Bram said "walk it like you've been asked," and I chose to be seen on Rope Street — hat off, cloak on, a man with somewhere to be — when Mask of Many Faces was right there and I could have gone in as a ropemaker's cousin. That one I'd do again. The Guild man waiting at the bottom of the street is a conversation I want to have. But I noticed myself choosing the hard road because it made a better scene rather than because James would, and that's worth watching.

A low chest sits at the foot of the bed with its lid up and nothing in it. Pegs for clothes run along one wall, and in the corner a curtain hangs on a rod over a shallow alcove. You check the alcove first. It holds a chamber pot and a broom and nothing else. You crouch to look under the bed. There's barely a hand's width of space and a lot of dust, and nobody could fit there. The chest is too small for anyone but a child.

The cat jumps down while you look. He makes his own round, nose low along the skirting, along the bed frame and under the curtain. Nothing he finds bothers him. Through the bond you get stale tobacco from some earlier lodger, mice in the wall, and the faint sour smell of whoever scrubbed the floor. None of it is the pepper and lamp-oil.

The window is a single casement under the eaves. It has small panes of cloudy glass in lead and a pair of wooden shutters inside. When you open the shutters you can see that the casement's latch is a plain iron hook dropped into an eye. The frame has warped enough to leave a gap along the edge where the two meet, wide enough to slide a thin knife-blade through. Through the glass you see a lean-to roof of wet slate about six feet below the sill, probably the kitchen. It slopes down to an alley where a single lamp burns at the far end. A man could climb onto that roof from the alley with a barrel and some nerve, or come down onto it from the roofline.

The bolt on the door, though, is as good as Mags said. It's a heavy iron slide on a new plate, screwed into the frame. The wood around the screws is still pale where it was freshly cut. You shoot it home, and it seats with a solid clunk you feel through your hand.

Somewhere in the wall behind the bed, the singing goes on. It's slow and soft, the same few phrases round and round. The cat jumps onto the blankets, turns once and sits facing the window.

The wrapped card goes on the near side of the bed and the deck on the far side, with the whole straw tick between them. The rod lies along the frame where his hand can find it in the dark.

The cat watches all this from the blankets. When the request comes down the bond he doesn't look round. What comes back is short and plain: *yes*. His gaze stays on the window.

The coin is cool under James's thumb. He says the words to the ceiling and the soot-black beams, and the singing in the wall goes on as if nobody spoke. He lies down. Sleep comes slowly, then all at once, the way it does after a long road.

He dreams of a table. It isn't a card table. There are no cards and no players, only green baize under one lamp. A gold coin stands on its edge in the middle of the cloth and spins. It spins for a long time without slowing or wobbling, and it doesn't fall. Every time the lamplight catches one face it's gone before he can see which face it was. Someone across the table is waiting for it to fall. He can't see who, only that they're patient.

Down in the real world the Elfsong empties and goes quiet. The common room shuts below him. A late door bangs. Somewhere past midnight the singing in the wall thins and stops.

A little before the half-hour, a man comes over the lean-to roof.

The cat hears him first. One slate shifts under a careful boot and clicks against the slate below it. It's a small sound, but nothing else in the building is making any.

James wakes all at once, without the grogginess. The jolt down the bond feels like claws in his mind, and the green table is gone. It's dark. The bedroll still hangs over the door, and the passage beyond it is silent. On the blankets by his knee the cat has gone flat, with his ears pinned forward at the shutters. What comes through the bond is sharp and close: *one. outside. on the roof.* A moment later a breath of wet air leaks in around the warped frame, and the cat adds a smell. It's wet leather and tar, and under them something sour and nervous. It isn't pepper, and it isn't lamp-oil. It isn't Jory.

Something scrapes on the other side of the shutters. It's thin and metallic, a blade sliding into the gap between the casement and its frame and feeling for the hook. It stops. Whoever it is heard nothing from inside and is listening. Then the blade starts again, slowly.

The shutters are still fastened, and the basin still sits under them. The man outside hasn't got the hook up yet.

The owner of this game would like a note from you, as the player who sat at this table: what worked, what broke, what was missing. In your own words.

I enjoyed playing James here. The strongest parts were the atmosphere, the NPCs, and the way small choices led naturally into trouble. I ended the session wanting to meet Mother Tessaly and find out what the card meant.

**What worked**
- The NPCs had distinct voices and interests. Varn’s guarded professionalism, Tamsin’s salesmanship, and Jory’s polite evasions made conversations worth having.
- James’s background mattered immediately. The offered card game tested his promise without forcing him to break it, and the cat was a useful companion with personality.
- I could solve problems by talking and taking precautions. Calling the follower into the Watch’s light and warning the burglar both worked without becoming compulsory fights.
- Concrete details supported decisions: closing gates, the dawn appointment, the window latch, and the accessible roof. That makes me hopeful about the eventual heist.

**What broke**
- The roll system repeatedly used **+2 instead of +7** for Persuasion and Intimidation. Narration corrected the results, but the displayed record remained wrong. Worse, my correction couldn’t reach the GM until I pressed Onward. There needs to be a way to flag a bad roll while its card is pending.
- The burglary scene was narrated in full, then paused for a check about something that had already happened, then repeated almost verbatim after the roll. Resolve checks at the point of uncertainty, before narrating their consequences.
- Interface updates leaked information James hadn’t learned: “Guild Sneak on the Roof” and the Guild faction tag effectively identified the intruder’s affiliation while the story said I hadn’t discovered who sent him.
- The opening character record contradicted the supplied sheet and campaign rules in places, notably rapier proficiency, the Healing Light limit, and attunement. Those discrepancies need settling before play.

**What was missing or could improve**
- **More progress per turn.** An entire session covered arrival, several conversations, supper, and part of a night. Those scenes were good individually, but the larger premise barely came into view. I wanted to reach at least the first substantial briefing about Tymora’s task.
- Routine transactions could be compressed. The gold-to-silver-to-copper exchanges received more attention than they needed.
- Out-of-game explanations were often longer than necessary, especially explanations of why ordinary actions required no roll. A short correction is useful; a numbered audit of opening a window interrupts the mood.
- The details of precautions need to stay physically consistent. I intended the basin to fall noisily if the shutters opened; the narration placed it on the floor while still treating it as that alarm.
- The mystery offered several warnings and withheld answers in succession. A firm, actionable discovery sooner would give me more to plan around.

Overall: a compelling city and good character interaction, held back by unreliable roll integration, occasional information leaks, and slow pacing. Keep the grounded NPCs and respect for player choices; tighten the routine scenes and let the central adventure arrive sooner.
Was there a moment you wanted to do something and didn't? Which?

Yes—the clearest was retrieving and examining the burglar’s dagger. I’d lit the roof and checked the alley specifically to work out a safe way to recover it. Then the session ended. I wanted to turn that intrusion into something I could investigate, rather than just another warning that someone was interested in me.

I also wanted to challenge the incorrect Persuasion modifier **before accepting the roll’s outcome**. I tried, but the interface wouldn’t send my message while the card was pending. Pressing Onward felt like accepting a result I knew was wrong, even though the GM subsequently corrected it.

By contrast, not chasing the burglar was deliberate: James had an important dawn appointment and wasn’t going to scramble onto wet slates just because somebody ran. That felt like a character choice, not a restriction.

James doesn't move from the dark of the room. Through the bond he sends the order down, fast and quiet: *to her, keep low, take her sleeve.*

Under the loading stage something small and grey moves. Penny doesn't go out along the waterline, where the post-lamp falls. She goes up the face of the wall into the black strip under its lip, the strip that hid Tamsin, belly to the stone. She has thirty feet of shadow to cover, and the lamp is ten paces off.

Penny is just gone. James knows where she is only because he feels her through the bond. On his own he'd never find her: no grey shape against the stone, no eyeshine, not even a shadow out of place. She runs the black strip under the wall's lip in one long stretch, pauses once when the buoy rings, and is in the stair corner before the stroke has died away.

She puts her head under Tamsin's hand, the one pressed flat on her coat, and pushes up hard, the way a cat demands to be stroked. Tamsin flinches and nearly cries out, then sees what it is.

James sees her face in what little light reaches the corner. She knows the cat. She looks up the wall, past the nets, to the roof shutter standing open a hand's width on a dark room. Her mouth goes tight.

Penny takes a mouthful of patched sleeve in her teeth and pulls back towards the stone, steady, not letting go.

For a long moment Tamsin stays up on her knees. Then she lets herself be pulled. She sinks back down into the corner until she's a lump of dark under the lip of the wall, one arm round the cat and the other hand back on her coin. She doesn't take her eyes off the water's edge. Penny settles against her ribs and stays there.

At the head of the steps the lamp priestess hasn't turned her head. The light stays narrow on the river.

Down at the water's edge, the salt priestess brings her hand out of her sleeve. In it is a short, flat blade with a stubby tip, the kind fishwives use to open oysters. She doesn't hurry. With the other hand she tips the young man's head back against the weed. She sets the blade between his front teeth, gives it a small twist, and the jaw opens with a sound James doesn't hear but can see in her shoulders.

She puts two fingers into the dead mouth and draws out something small and dark. It catches the post-lamp once as it comes out, a quick brown glint of copper.

Something warms against James's ribs, inside his coat, in the pocket where he keeps the gangplank coin on its own. It isn't hot, just warm, like a hand laid flat against him through the cloth. It lasts the space of a breath and then fades.

The salt priestess doesn't look at the coin. She drops it into a small lidded box at her belt, pale wood or bone, with salt already in it, and shuts the lid. Then she takes a pinch from the sack beside her and puts it on the dead man's tongue where the coin was. She pushes his jaw closed with the heel of her hand and holds it there.

She speaks to the water again, low and steady. This time the slack air carries a little more of it up to the window. Not all of it, but one phrase comes up twice, in the same flat, careful voice, the way a clerk reads back a sum:

"*…paid, and carried. Paid, and carried.*"

She stands, wipes the oyster knife on her robe, and looks up the steps.

"Hobb."

The cart-man lets go of the shafts and goes down. He's heavy on the black, weedy stone, but sure-footed, and he passes within an arm's reach of the corner where Tamsin is lying. He doesn't look into it. He bends at the bottom, gets his arms under the young fisherman's shoulders and knees, and lifts him out of the water in one heave. Water streams off the knitted jersey and slaps on the steps.

At the top, the lamp priestess has finally turned from the river. She lifts the hood a finger's width and sends the light down the stairs ahead of Hobb's feet, to show him the way up. The pale blade climbs the steps one by one, the dry flights and then the corner under the wall's lip, and comes over it.

It slides over a heap of dark rags in the corner. Then it slides back.

Penny is sitting in the mouth of the arch with her back to them, watching the lane. James looks past her. A cooper's boy is rolling a hoop the wrong way up the street, half asleep, and the woman who shouted for trays is beating flour out of a cloth with her back to them both. Nobody is looking into a dark arch where there's nothing to see.

James lets the spell go.

It doesn't fade. It just stops. There's a girl beside him, smaller than her voice made her seem, still holding his hand hard. Tamsin looks down at her own feet, then at her free hand, and turns it over twice as if checking that she got the right one back.

"Huh," she says. She lets go of him and wipes the hand on her coat.

Pell's is a hatch in a whitewashed wall at the bend, with a board across it and a steaming tray on the board. Pell is a narrow woman with flour to the elbows and a face like a shut door. She looks at James, looks at the cat, and looks for longest at the barefoot girl standing just behind his elbow.

"Two a copper."

James puts down two coppers. Pell slides four rolls across the board, brown and split on top and too hot to hold. She watches Tamsin take three of them and tuck two away inside her coat. Without a word she breaks a heel off a burnt loaf behind the hatch and puts it on the board as well, nearer the girl than the man. Then she turns back to her ovens.

Tamsin takes the heel too. She doesn't say thank you, but she eats it first.

They go back the way they came, across the fish market, which is waking now with handcarts, wet sacking and a man hosing scales off the boards with a bucket, and then up the left-hand lane. It's ordinary in daylight: net-sheds on one side and the long low roof of the rope-walk on the other, with a smell of hemp and hot tar. At the head of the lane the shell-crusted doors of the Water Queen's House catch the first grey light. Above its yard wall the smoke is thinner now, a pale thread going straight up.

Tamsin chooses the spot. It's the lower end of the rope-walk, where the shed stands open on a yard of coiled cable and an upturned hand-barrow. She sits on the barrow in plain sight of the lane, eating her second roll slowly, as if she has all morning. James stays a few paces back against the shed post, where the eaves throw some shade. Penny goes up onto the coil of cable and pretends to sleep.

The bells up the hill ring half past five. A little after, the narrow gate in the yard wall opens and closes, and Hobb comes down the lane alone.

He walks the way he pulls the cart, head down and shoulders forward. There's a grey smear of ash down the front of his sailcloth smock, and his big hands are white to the wrists with dried salt. He's nearly level with the rope-walk before he lifts his head.

He sees the girl on the barrow first. He stops.

He looks at her for a long moment: at the roll in her hand, at her bare feet. Then his eyes move to the shed post, and to the man standing by it. He knows the face. James can see that he does.

Hobb doesn't come closer, and he doesn't walk on. He looks back once up the lane at the blue doors, then at the girl again.

"Holt's girl," he says. His voice is low and rough from not being used. He moves his head a fraction towards James. "Window."

Then he steps off the lane, under the rope-walk's eaves, out of sight of the Water Queen's House, and stands there with his salt-white hands hanging, waiting.

"They look down this lane," he says. "Back of the shed."

I follow him behind the shed, keeping my hands clear of my weapons, and wait until we’re out of sight of the lane.

“James Worgen. Thank you for keeping quiet about us.”

I keep my voice low. “I saw them take a copper from that man’s mouth. Tamsin’s father had one too. What does ‘paid and carried’ mean, Hobb?”

Behind the rope-walk the shed's back wall runs along a strip of beaten earth. Tar barrels stand there in a row, and a ladder climbs to a loft door that hangs half open. The lane is gone from sight, and so are the blue doors. Hobb stops by the barrels, puts his back to the boards and lets his hands hang. Up close he smells of smoke and wet salt, and something sweeter under both that James doesn't want to name.

Tamsin comes round the corner of the shed a few steps behind them. She stops where she can see both of them and the way out. Penny hasn't come. Through the bond James can feel her still lying on the cable coil, her attention on the lane.

At *thank you* Hobb's head dips once. It isn't really a nod.

At *paid and carried* he says nothing for a while. He looks at the ground between his boots.

"Don't know." His voice is low and rough. "They say it. Every time. Same words." He rubs his thumb over the dried salt on the back of one hand, and it flakes off white. "Ask them, they'll say Umberlee's due. Sea gets her copper."

Then he lifts his head, and he isn't looking at James. He's looking at the girl.

"Your da. I carried him." A pause. "Careful."

Tamsin's hand goes flat against her coat. She doesn't say anything. Her chin comes up.

Hobb turns back to James. Now that he has started, the words come one after another, slowly, the way he'd stack crates.

"Every one I carried. Had money that week." He holds up a thick finger. "Holt. Silver at bones. Whole lane knew." A second finger. "This one tonight. Wyl. Netted a run of bass Tenday. Sold it all. Stood drinks." He lowers his hand. "Poor men. Lucky once. Then the steps."

He lets that hang for a moment and doesn't say what he thinks of it. His eyes go up towards the corner of the shed, where the smoke from the yard is thinning to a pale thread against a grey sky.

"In the yard, salt and fire. Box goes in the kiln. Most come out black. Crumble." He shakes his head once. "Some don't. One in ten, maybe. Comes out clean. Like new." His jaw works. "Old one keeps those. Lamp. Locked box. Don't know where they go after."

He looks at James's coat, at the place over his ribs where nothing shows, and then away again, as if he's decided not to ask.

"Holt's mouth was empty." He says it to Tamsin, quietly. "Old one asked who'd been at him. Asked Fist. Asked fish market. Nobody said." He breathes out through his nose. "She don't forget a thing missing."

Tamsin goes very still.

Hobb pushes off the boards and puts a hand on the ladder. The salt on his knuckles is white against the dark wood. He stops there and looks at James, slowly and squarely, for the first time.

"Window. Then gone, in the lane." It isn't a question, and it doesn't sound like an accusation either. "Whatever you are. Keep her off the steps. Next low water, they'll look harder."

He waits on the bottom rung for an answer.

The owner of this game would like a note from you, as the player who sat at this table: what worked, what broke, what was missing. In your own words.

What worked best was the atmosphere and the people. The wet quay, Wenna’s netting needle, Pell quietly adding bread, and Hobb saying he carried Tamsin’s father “careful” made the city feel inhabited. Hobb choosing not to report us was the strongest moment: an NPC making a consequential choice without explaining himself.

Tamsin gave me a reason to care immediately. Her knowledge was useful, her recklessness believable, and she pushed back rather than becoming an obedient quest marker. Penny also felt genuinely useful—scouting, distracting, and helping Tamsin—without solving everything automatically. The rescue with upcast Invisibility was a satisfying payoff for using my character’s abilities.

What broke or felt rough:
- The rolls need a mechanical audit. Deception was listed as +7 but rolled at +4. The sheet also contradicted the campaign files on Healing Light, rapier proficiency, and attunement. Some discrepancies follow ordinary 5e, but the agreed campaign overrides should be applied consistently.
- The failed Investigation result was explained twice, including narration that James kept searching without my choosing that. Resolve failure once and move on.
- Tamsin repeatedly moving towards danger created tension, but after several successive near-discoveries it began to feel like a mechanism for keeping the scene escalating. I’d like opportunities for precautions to buy a clean success or some breathing room.
- The opening clock was confusing: arrival near sunset became half past eleven after relatively little elapsed activity.

What was missing was more specifically **James**. This was a strong harbour mystery, but his mandate from Tymora—and the promised crew-building heist—remained distant. The warm coin and card dealer were intriguing signals; soon I’d want a concrete lead connecting this trouble to his mission. Not the twist or the full explanation, just enough direction to begin making plans.

Overall, I was engaged and would continue. Keep the grounded NPCs, fair opportunities to avoid combat, and mysteries revealed through observable actions. Tighten the rules bookkeeping, give successful plans room to work, and bring James’s particular purpose into focus next session.
Was there a moment you wanted to do something and didn't? Which?

Yes—when Mirelle showed me the card with its face worn away exactly like the copper.

I wanted to walk over and ask, “Where did you get that card?” Not play a hand, but test whether she knew about Tymora’s ban, the coin, or why I’d arrived. That felt like a hook aimed specifically at James, rather than a mystery he happened to encounter.

I followed Tamsin instead because her fear and her father’s death were more urgent. Once she was repeatedly in danger, going back to question a card dealer would have felt like abandoning her.

That was my choice, not something you prevented. But I did want a quiet interval afterward to pursue Mirelle. Her packing up made me wonder whether that opportunity was disappearing while I followed the other lead.

I nod slowly and keep my voice as low as his.

"Nothing to your door tonight. I won't touch the lock, I won't leave a mark, and nobody will know I was down there except you and me." I glance at the bolt behind him, then back at his face. "You've got my word on that, for what a stranger's word is worth. I'd rather have them come back to a store that looks exactly as they left it."

I lean a shoulder on the wall beside the stove so I'm not crowding him.

"Few more questions, and then I'm gone. When did the thin man last pay you? When's he due again? How long has he had the store, since the first week with the lock? And when the boat comes after one, does anything go in or out? Crates, sacks, people?" I pause. "And the girl. When did you see her last, before today?"

I give him a short, tired smile, the honest kind this time.

"And your name, friend. If this goes bad, I'd like to know whose door to knock on to tell you so, before they do."

*To the cat:* *Go out the gap and sit somewhere high where you can see the stair and the water. Don't go down. If a boat comes, tell me.*

The net-mender listens with his back against the bolt. When James promises *nothing to your door*, the big man's eyes narrow a little, the way a man checks a coin's weight in his palm. He says nothing about the word. He doesn't spit on it either.

At James's boot the cat gets up, walks to the door and sits facing the bolt. The net-mender looks down at it, then at James. He grunts, slides the bolt back a hand's width and lets the door open just wide enough. The cat flows through the gap and is gone. He shuts it and shoots the bolt again.

"Cat's got manners," he mutters. "More than most."

Through the bond James feels the cat leave the doorway, go up the side of the shack, over the salt-stiff nets and onto the roof. It settles there with the river sliding black below. From the ridge it can see the head of the stair and, past the parapet, the open water down to the landing. *High. Watching.*

The net-mender scratches his beard with the needle hand and answers the questions in order, slowly, as if he's counting them off.

"Paid today. Before dusk. Came up the stair, put the five down, went back down. Girl was with him." His mouth works. "Heard oars after. Early. Not the woman's stroke. Him rowing, maybe. Don't know."

"Due again in a tenday. Same as always. Ten days."

"Had the store since the ice went off the river. Spring. Three months, four. Lock went on the first week."

He stops at the boat. His eyes go to the floor, toward the water.

"Don't look. Hear, though. Floor's thin." He breathes through his nose. "Sacks, mostly. Dragged. Something clinks, sometimes, like a crock. And twice…" He stops, and his jaw works. "Twice it was heavy. Two of them on it, going in. Grunting. Stink was worse after, three days." He shakes his head once, hard. "Not my business. Told myself."

"Girl. Four, five days back, before today. Up on the bridge, the Rock end, by the eel stalls. Chalk on her fingers. Didn't look at me." He pauses. "Thin. Thinner than spring."

Then there's the name. He takes his time with it. He looks at James's face, then at the honest tired smile, and his weight settles onto his good leg.

"Gask," he says finally. "Everyone on the bridge knows Gask. Ask anyone for the net-mender with the foot." He reaches back and puts his hand on the bolt without drawing it. "You knock twice. Like you did. Not the Fist way."

He doesn't open the door yet.

"You staying about for the boat?" His voice drops even lower. "Not in here. Not on my stair."

"Not on your stair," I agree. "Not in here. You won't see me again tonight, Gask, and neither will they."

I push off the wall and wait for him to draw the bolt. On the step I pause, half turned, and keep it low:

"If he comes early, or the girl comes up alone, don't do anything. Just be a man mending nets. That's the safest thing in the world to be."

Then I'm back on the bridge, hands in my pockets, a tired traveller who's finally found his bearings. I walk toward the Rock end, past the eel stalls where he last saw the girl, looking for somewhere I can sit for hours without anyone wondering why. A tavern or cookshop with a window or a bench on the downstream side would be best, somewhere I can see the open water below the span and the landing's side of the river. If I find one, I'll buy a bowl of whatever's hot and a small beer I'll make last, and sit with my back to the wall.

*Stay on the roof,* I send to the cat. *Rest if you like, but keep one ear on the water. When oars come, wake me. I want to see the boat, which way it comes from and which way it goes, and how many are in it. Nothing more.*

Before I settle in, I pull the hood of the grey cloak up and use the Mask to blunt my face a little. Ten years older, a broken nose, a beard going grey. Gask has seen my real face, and that's enough people for one night.

Gask draws the bolt. He holds the door open just wide enough for a man and looks past James at the dark gap beside his shack. While James says his piece, the big man's jaw works.

"Man mending nets," he mutters, as if trying out the words. Then he looks James in the eye. "Go on, then."

The door shuts behind James and the bolt slides home. A moment later the twine starts rasping through the mesh again, slow and steady.

On the bridge the evening is winding down. The fishwife's stall is folded and roped. A boy is going along the lantern hooks with a taper, lighting the ones that have gone out. James puts his hands in his pockets and walks toward Wyrm's Rock at the pace of a man with nowhere he has to be.

*Stay on the roof,* he sends. *Rest if you like…*

*Roof,* the cat sends back, and he feels it settle on the ridge with its paws tucked under.

About thirty paces on, past a shuttered chandler's and a cookfire with three porters squatting around it, the bond starts to thin. The cat's steady attention fades like a voice behind a closing door. At forty paces he can't hear it at all. The cat is still there, he knows that much, but whatever he sends now won't reach it, and nothing it sends will reach him.

The eel stalls are at the Rock end, where the bridge widens around the fortress's bulk. Four of them stand in a row, two still open, their tubs of black water seething with what's left of the day's catch. There's no girl and no grey shawl, only a man with a cleaver and a woman scrubbing a board. Chalk would show up well on these stones, and there's none.

Just past the stalls, a cookshop has been built out over the downstream parapet on timber brackets. It's a low, steamy room with a painted board showing an eel tied in a knot. The back wall is mostly shutters, propped open on the river. James stops in the shadow of the doorpost, pulls up the hood of his old regimental cloak and runs a thumb along his jaw. The Mask does its work without a sound. The face under the hood gains ten years, a nose broken and badly set, and a beard going grey at the corners. A Fist veteran on half pay, if anyone asks, and nobody here will.

Inside it smells of pepper, eel fat and wet wool. A heavyset woman with her sleeves pinned up stirs a pot the size of a cartwheel and doesn't look up. "Stew's eel. Beer's small. Eight copper the pair, bowl back when you're done."

He counts eight coppers onto the board, every one he has. She slops a bowl full and draws the beer, and he takes both to the bench along the back wall. Through the open shutters the Chionthar runs black and wide toward the harbour. Riding lights on moored barges bob downstream, and further off the Seatower's beacon smears red on the water. If he leans to the left he can see back along the span toward the city end, a dark row of piers going away from him. Somewhere among them is Gask's landing. From here it's just more dark.

The stew is better than it looks. The beer is thin enough to make last all night.

At the next table two watermen with tar to the elbows are working through a jug.

"…by the Seatower, Tuesday. Fist hooked him out with a boathook."

"Coin in his teeth?"

"Coin in his teeth." The older one drinks. "My sister's girl does the floors at the Water Queen's House. Says the priestesses won't have them. Fist brought one up there in the spring, proper, for the offering, and the high one wouldn't touch it. Said it was never paid to Her." He sets the cup down. "Funny old coin, the girl said. Face on both sides."

"Face on both sides," the younger one says, and laughs, though not as if he finds it funny. "Lucky."

"Was lucky. Won forty gold on the dogs the week before, I heard."

They move on to the price of pitch. The cook scrapes her pot. Out on the river an oar dips once and goes quiet, a barge hand going home.

Jory takes the silver to the cartwheel pot and comes back with the jug full and no change. Nobody mentions it. The older man pours for all three and pushes a cup across.

"Hob," he says, by way of a name. "My sister's girl, Nessa, that's who saw it. Fist brought one up to the Water Queen's House in the spring, wrapped in a rag like it was holy. Priestess wouldn't put a finger to it." He drinks. "A woman's face, Nessa said. Same woman both sides. Laughing on the one and weeping on the other. Like she couldn't make up her mind." He sets the cup down. "Nessa didn't like it. Said the high one went and washed her hands after, and she'd never touched it."

"Your sergeant," Jory says. "The one who never lost a toss. Did they fish him out too?"

Hob gives him a look, and Jory shuts up and drinks.

"Tuesday's one was Fenn Corlis," Hob says. "Lighterman. Worked the barges same as us, never had two coppers to rub together. Then a tenday back he puts his whole wage on a dog at the Rivington pits, a dog with three legs that works, and it wins. Then another. Forty gold by the end of it." He shakes his head. "Spent half of it at the Blushing Mermaid, buying rounds for men who never bought him one. Walking about like the Lady had him by the hand. Then Tuesday the Fist has him on a boathook by the Seatower, blue as a mussel, with a coin in his teeth."

James listens for the rest: a long face, grey hands, a woman at the oars, the smell of burnt horn. He gets most of one.

"Fenn wouldn't have gone in the water drunk," Jory says. "Swam like an eel. Showed off about it." He turns his cup round. "River's full of fools at night anyway. That skiff with no lamp, for one. Comes up under the Crossing late, woman at the oars, and goes back down toward the harbour before light. Near took my oar off in the spring, and she never said a word. Didn't even look round."

"Lots of folk row without a lamp," Hob says, not quite to Jory. "Not our business who."

About the man with grey hands, or the stink, neither of them has a word. They've moved on to the price of pitch by the time James finishes his beer. He thanks them, takes his bowl back to the cook, who doesn't look up, and goes out onto the bridge.

The bridge has emptied while he ate. The lanterns hang further apart than they seemed at dusk, with stretches of dark between them where the light doesn't meet. Walking back toward the city end, James counts doorways and finds what he wants: a stretch of the downriver parapet between two lanterns, with a squat stone post where an old chain once hung. The shack's roof is a dark hump against the sky about 75 feet back along the span. He settles onto the stones with his back against the post, pulls his cloak round him and lets his head drop the way a man's does when beer has beaten him.

The bond comes clear like a door opening onto a warm room.

*I'm back. Same orders. Oars, you wake me.*

*Roof,* the cat sends. Then, after a pause that might be disapproval: *Cold.*

Time goes by. The Mask's hour runs out a little after nine, and James renews it under the cloak with a thumb along his jaw: the same broken nose, the same grey beard, nothing a passerby would notice changing. He does it again after ten. The eel stalls shut. The porters' cookfire burns down to a red smear and the porters roll themselves in sacking beside it. At the city end, Pell's lantern goes out, and a little later the patter stops.

A little after eleven, boots come along the bridge from the barrier. Two of them, in red-trimmed gear, walking the way men walk at the end of a long shift. Their lantern swings toward the post and stops on him. One of them prods his boot with the butt of a spear.

"Oi. Grandad. You got a bed?"

James gives them what a drunk gives: a slow lift of the head, a squint into the light, a wet grumble about Tethyr and a sergeant who owed him money.

The answer is slow, like a cat getting up when it would rather not. *Edge. Low. Not down.* There's a pause. *You. Also.* He feels it accept the orders, and he also feels it decide that the nets smell of tar and it will put up with them.

Time passes. A gull complains somewhere toward the Rock and gives up. The porters by the dead cookfire snore out of step with each other. Twice James feels the cat's attention prick toward the water and settle again. The first time it's a fish turning. The second time it's the loose board downstream, knocking.

Wyrm's Rock rings one. The single stroke rolls out over the water, and the bridge seems to hold still while it fades.

*Oars.* The word comes with the sound itself, heard through the cat's ears before James's own catch anything. It slides down the roof's slope toward the river side and wedges in under the fringe of a hanging net, where the salt-stiff mesh breaks up its outline. Its chin touches the edge of the boards. Below it the landing is a grey shelf in a black hole.

Then part of the dark moves against the rest, a long low shape with no lamp, coming upstream close under the bridge piers where the barges' riding lights don't reach. Through the cat he hears it arrive: the hiss of the hull losing speed, a soft bump of wood on stone. Then comes a rope's dry rasp as someone runs it through the iron ring and draws it tight.

Up on the roof the cat stops breathing, as cats do. Behind the shack wall, Gask's cot doesn't creak. He's awake and lying very still.

The boat is tied up at the landing. Nobody has spoken yet.

*Post,* the cat sends back. It's a grudging word, but it means yes.

Then he goes down the bond, and the bridge goes away. His own body is still there: cold stone under his hips, the rod in his hand. But it's blind and deaf now, a coat left hanging on a peg. Through the cat he has tar in his nose, the scratch of salt-stiff mesh across one ear, and boards against his chin. Below him is the landing, a grey shelf at the bottom of a black well, and the long dark shape of a skiff lying alongside it.

A cat's eyes don't do much better than a man's under that span. For a few heartbeats it's all shapes: the hull, a figure standing up in it, a bulk in the stern that moves.

Then someone lifts the hood of a lantern a finger's width.

The light is no wider than a blade, but it's aimed low across the landing, and the cat's eyes have been wide open in the dark for an hour. The glare hits them like a slap. The cat flinches, its eyes screw shut and water, and through the bond James sees nothing but a smeared orange blot with black shapes swimming in it. When the cat can see again, the moment has passed. He has nothing he could swear to: no faces, no hands, and no idea who had the key or how the lock opened. There's only a seam of lamplight where the pier door now stands ajar, and two figures on the landing with their backs to the roof. One stands upright with her arms folded, the rower. The other, longer, is bent over at the door.

The skiff's stern is still a heap of shadow. Something there shifts. It's either a second, smaller shape pressed against a sack or just the sack slumping, and the cat can't tell which. Then comes a cough, small and quickly smothered, as if a hand had gone over a mouth. It came from the stern, or maybe from the door.

James's sight fails him, but his ears still work.

The long figure doesn't go in. He straightens, and the blade of lantern light swings off the door and down onto the weed. Nothing has been dropped on the ground under the window, and the hard earth has no fresh marks on it, only the old ruts of someone carrying wood. A sparrow lands on the wall, looks at nothing and flies off again.

Across the yard the upper window of the next house is just as it was in the night. The shutters are closed and warped, with a black gap down the middle. He watches that gap for a slow count of thirty. No light shows behind it and nothing moves. If anyone is standing back from it in the dark, he can't see them. Below it, the rag still plugs the broken pane, grey with old smoke.

Nothing living is out there except the sparrow, and it has gone.

He lifts the latch. The shutter swings out a hand's width on a dry hinge, and the cold morning comes in smelling of woodsmoke and the yard. The cat leans forward over the gap at once, its nose almost on the outside edge of the frame, its whiskers pushed forward.

That's the end of it. James goes up the stair.

The stair is old and narrow and turns twice. Every tread creaks a different note. The Boots of Elvenkind make no sound on any of them, so only the wood talks. At the second floor a passage runs back along the house under a sloping ceiling, with doors on one side and the smell of lamp oil and old beeswax. Six is at the end, as she said. The key turns hard, and the bolt inside is a good iron one that goes home with a solid clack.

The room is about what two nights' money buys. There's a narrow bed with a bolster, a washstand with a chipped jug, a table and one chair, a lamp, a row of pegs, and a small rag rug that someone once cared about. The ceiling comes down at a slant over the bed, low enough that a tall man would learn about it in the night.

He goes to the window first. It's a casement with small leaded panes and a latch that sticks before it gives. Below is the yard he crossed coming in: cobbles, the worn lintel's lamp throwing a yellow fan over the door, and the mouth of the hops-smelling lane at the far side. It's a long drop to the cobbles, fifteen feet or a bit more, onto stone. A little to the left and about six feet down, though, is the mossy slate roof of a woodshed built against the wall. A man could let himself down onto that from the sill without a rope, and onto a water butt at the corner from there. Nobody is in the yard. A cart stands empty by the brewery wall with its shafts on the ground.

Then he lays out the room the way a careless man would. He opens the pack on the bed and leaves the bedroll half out. The crossbow and the quiver of bolts lean in the corner where the door would show them to anyone who looked in. He spreads the pay slip flat on the table under the lamp, *James Worgen* face up in a regimental clerk's tidy hand. The promissory note and the deck go back inside his jacket, against his ribs. The rod, the cloak, the coin on its cord and the two red potions stay where they are.

He sits on the bed with his back to the wall, under the slope of the ceiling, and reaches down the bond.

For a while there's nothing, only the far, cottony silence of a link stretched past where it can carry. The common room's noise comes up through the floorboards: a laugh, a chair scraping. Somewhere along the passage a door opens and closes. Then, a little before the three-quarter hour, the bond catches like a fish taking a line.

What comes first is a jumble of road, the way it always comes when the cat is moving fast: cobbles, a gutter, the hops wall, and below all of it the cat's pleasure at being out and running with a job to do. Then the memory, pushed at him whole, the way a cat brings you something it's caught. There's lantern heat on its back and boot leather under it, a worn boot that smells of horse and the bridge, and a woman's voice just above. The voice isn't speaking to him. It's counting under its breath along with the tail on the stone, one, two, up to six, and then a seventh beat where the tail stops and nothing comes.

*"Six,"* in that flat checkpoint voice. Then the boot shifts under it, slowly, the way you move a foot when something is sitting on it that you've decided not to kick.

So Varn has her six.

Behind that comes the bridge, seen from the gate at cat height, all legs and wheels and lamplight in a long line. There's Tobin's barrel and its lamp, still lit. Tobin is under it and shuffling, and the smell coming off him is sharper than it was at dusk, like sweat gone cold. Past him, three hundred feet down the Crossing toward the black hump of the Rock, the cat shows him something it noticed because it was different. At dusk a lamp on an iron arm hung over the gap by the rope-maker's. Now there's only the arm. The gap is dark, a missing tooth in the row of lit shopfronts, and the head of the stair is somewhere inside it.

The cat doesn't know what that means, and doesn't pretend to. It only knows the place has changed, so it brings it to him.

Then the common room arrives through its eyes, warm and close: the door, the dwarves' boots, the hearthstone. In the corner, the velvet collar sits straight-backed, both hands on the wood, with no dice in them. The cat turns twice on the warm stone and lies down facing the corner. The bond settles into something low and steady. *Here. Watching.*

James stands, faces the dark window glass and lets the Lady's mask come over him.

It takes a few muttered words and a pass of the hand down the face. Nobody would remember it as anything if they saw it. In the glass, a different man looks back at him. He's a Rivington boatman, broader in the face and older, with grey through a short beard and a nose that has been out in a lot of weather. The Tethyrian cloak is gone. In its place is a dockhand's canvas jacket, tar-stained at the cuffs, with the collar turned up and a knitted cap pulled down. His boots look like boots that have stood in bilge water. The coin on its cord has vanished under a collar that isn't there. Beneath it all, the cloak still hangs from his shoulders, light and real, and the old enchantment in it sits close and quiet as ever.

Below him the common room goes on, loud and yellow. The way down is the stair he came up. It ends at the foot of the room, in full view of the bar and of Hesper, who wrote *James Worgen* in her book an hour ago and has watched everyone who has gone up those stairs tonight. The other way is the window, the woodshed and the yard.

It's about ten to ten.

He gets nothing from it. The gap is a slot of black between two lit fronts. At a walking pace, with his eyes on it for three strides and no more, he can make out the iron arm against the lesser dark of the sky and nothing else. He can't tell if the lamp still hangs from it. He can't see the loft hatch, or whether anyone is standing at the top of the stair. If someone is in there, he's walked past them at ten feet without knowing. The dark keeps all of it.

He walks on to the end of the eel stall and turns down the narrow slot behind it. The bridge's edge is here, a low parapet, and past it the Chionthar is black and moving. The crates are where he saw them at dusk, stacked three high against the stall's back wall and smelling strongly of eels. He goes up them quietly. The boots make no sound at all. The top crate does. It rocks under his hand as he puts his weight on it and knocks once against the back of the stall, a hollow wooden *tock* that the shutters swallow.

He freezes there for a breath, then goes on and lies flat on the roof. The tar is still faintly warm from the day. From here, through the gap in the fronts, he can see the top of the stair dropping away into darkness. Past the roof's back edge, if he cranes, there's the dark curve of the Rock's footing and the black mouth of the first arch over the water.

Something moves under him.

It's in the stall, under the boards, a foot from his chest: the scrape of a body sitting up on something hard, then the clink of metal against a tub. A voice comes up through the roof and the shutters. It's young, a girl's, pitched low and rough to sound bigger than it is.

"Who's that." It isn't quite a question. "I heard you. Get off my da's roof." A pause, and a breath drawn in through the teeth. "I've got the gaff, and I'll put it up through the boards, I will. Or I'll scream the Fist down off the gate. Which do you want?"

Somewhere behind him, three hundred feet back up the bridge, Tobin is still calling the Lady to passers-by. Below, the river goes on talking to the stones.

The coin goes still on the boards. For a breath nothing happens. Then the girl lets out a sound that is half a laugh, and James hears wood knock wood as she lays the gaff down on the tubs.

"Gods. A *whole* one." He hears the coin scrape on the boards as she picks it up, then a pause. He can guess she's biting it. "It's real."

When she speaks again she doesn't try to sound bigger than she is, and she sounds about thirteen.

"Rook. All right. I'm Dace." She sniffs. "Da named all of us after fish. Don't." Her voice comes closer to the boards, right under his ear. "You're not a boatman, neither. Boatmen climb like sacks. You came up them crates like a cat, all but the last one."

She doesn't wait for him to argue.

"The lamp's Pell's. Rope-maker." Her voice moves along under the roof, toward the gap. "He leaves it lit every night, all night, swears it keeps the hemp thieves off. Fourteen years Da's had this stall and Pell's never once let it go out. Tonight he shuts up at the eighth bell, climbs on his step, and pinches it out with his fingers. Didn't even wet them. He swore and sucked his thumb all the way down." A short breath. "Then he shuts the loft hatch. He never shuts it in summer, the hemp sweats. Then off home, Rivington way, quick."

She stops, and he can hear her deciding whether to tell the next part.

"This afternoon a man came up the stair. Up from the water, not down off the bridge. He stood in Pell's door and talked to him low, then gave him something, and Pell bit it like I bit yours." Her voice drops. "Big hands. Knitted cap like yours, pulled down. Didn't buy any rope. Went back down the stair, and I never heard a boat go off, so it was waiting somewhere under there."

The boards creak as she shifts on the tubs.

"And your boat, yeah. I've heard it. Not every night. Once a week, maybe, since spring." Her voice goes flat when she says *spring*. "You don't hear the oars. They wrap them. All you hear is the water dripping off, plip, plip, and the boat bumping the footing. Every waterman on this river sings or swears. That lot do neither." She doesn't say anything for a moment. "I heard her once. The woman. On the stair. She talks soft, like she's putting a baby down. I put my head under the blanket."

Then, brisker, like she's selling him something:

"There's an iron ring on the footing under the first arch. That's where they tie up, I've seen the rope marks on it in the morning. You won't see it from the middle of the roof. Go to the back corner, the left one, by the crates. Put your head over the edge and look down past the drainpipe. You can see the ring and a bit of water either side." A pause. "Don't fall off. Da'd never believe I didn't push you."

The coin goes somewhere safe. He hears the rustle of cloth and a blanket being pulled up.

"I'm not asleep," Dace says to the boards. "Just so you know. I'm lying here with the gaff."

James keeps the bottom treads in his eye. The grey cloak hasn't moved off its step. The hooded shape stops below her and shakes its head once. It doesn't say a word.

"No matter." Her voice comes up warm and unhurried, as if the cat had been a hope and not a need. "Cats come back to where they're fed."

Then she turns to Tobin. He's been standing so still that James had almost lost him against the stone.

"You looked at it, Tobin." She's gentle about it. "When you said *cat*. You looked straight up the stairs at it, like a little boy who's been told not to look at the cake." She waits. Tobin doesn't answer. "We don't look at things. Do we."

"No, lady." It comes out cracked.

A grey glove moves. James sees the purse come out on its drawstring, and he hears it before he sees anything else: one coin and then a second, falling from above into an open palm. It's gold, not rope.

"Two," she says. "One for him. One for being a good boy next time." The purse goes away. "Put it out tomorrow night, the same as always. If he comes back past your barrel, you'll tell me how he walks and who he's with. If he doesn't come back, you'll tell me that too."

She doesn't wait for him to say yes. She comes up the stair as she went down it, never hurrying. Her cloak catches the last of the hooded lantern's orange and loses it again. She passes under the eel stall roof close enough that James could drop his cap on her hood. He smells the cold ash again, and then she's out on the planking. She turns south toward the Rivington end, the way she came, and walks down the middle of the bridge with her gloved hands folded in front of her.

Under the arch, the hooded man edges back along the ledge with one hand on the wall. Rope scrapes through iron. A blade slips into the water, wrapped and silent, and the skiff moves off the footing. It drifts more than it rows, sliding away downstream on the current toward the harbour, hooded lantern and bag of stones and all. Within a few breaths it's only a darker patch on dark water, and then James can't tell it from the river.

Tobin is still on the landing. He's two steps from the bottom with his fist closed around two gold pieces, and he hasn't moved since she left.

From under the boards, so low it's almost nothing, comes Dace's voice: "She gone?"

The grey cloak is a pale smudge under the lamps toward Rivington, a hundred feet off and getting further. Down the bond the cat's heartbeat is slowing against Varn's boot, three hundred feet up the bridge the other way. It's a few minutes past midnight, and the boatman's face will hold until about a quarter to one.
