She is easy to keep in sight and hard to follow without being seen.

After midnight the Crossing is a long, bare street of planking between the shuttered fronts. Every third lamp still burns, and most of the doorways are dark. There's nobody to walk behind. James does it the only way an empty street allows: he doesn't follow her, he walks home along the same road. He keeps to the opposite side of the bridge, about a hundred feet back, and never passes under a lamp while she's under one. When she's in the light, he's in the dark between two lamps. When she steps out of it, he lets his own lamp take him for a few strides, cap down, a tired man in tarry canvas. The boots put him down on the old boards without a sound. Without them his heels would be the only noise on the whole bridge.

Halfway past the Rock she stops.

She doesn't turn her head. She stands at the rail with her gloved hands on it and looks downstream, toward the harbour, where the skiff went. She waits for as long as it takes to say a short prayer. James is between two lamps when she stops, and he stops too. He turns to the parapet, leans his forearms on it and spits into the river, the way men do on bridges at night. When she moves on, he gives her ten heartbeats and then moves on himself.

She never looks back. Twice, though, she slows under a lamp, the way you slow when you're listening behind you, and walks on when she hears nothing. James lets the gap open to a hundred and twenty feet and keeps it there.

The Rivington end of the bridge widens out into a cobbled square where the road comes down off the planking. There's a horse trough, a shuttered toll-house, and one lantern on a post by the trough. A man is sitting on the trough's edge with his elbows on his knees.

He stands up when she comes off the bridge. He's young and lanky, in a sailor's short coat with a scarf wound twice round his throat. She doesn't stop walking. He falls in beside her for six or seven strides, his head bent toward her hood, and James is too far off to hear a word of it. He sees her hand come out of the folded pair, palm down and level, the way you show a child how tall someone is. She moves it a little, once. The young man nods, and nods again. Then he turns back and walks onto the Crossing toward the city, whistling under his breath, his hands in his pockets.

That road runs right past James.

James is at the rail on the bridge's last stretch, cap down, doing what boatmen do with a river at night. The whistling comes up the planking. It's a sea tune, half the notes wrong. The young man passes at arm's length. Up close he's maybe twenty, with a long jaw, a chipped front tooth and the scarf pulled up to his chin. His eyes touch the Rivington boatman at the rail and slide off him, as they would off a post. Then he's gone north under the lamps, toward the Rock and the Basilisk Gate and the Lower City beyond it, at the pace of a man with an errand and no hurry about it.

James straightens up. The grey cloak is crossing the square.

She doesn't take the river road. She goes uphill, into the lanes of Rivington behind the waterfront, where the houses are wood on stone footings and lean together over streets too narrow for a cart. These streets are easier for him than the bridge was. They're crooked, half of them unlit, and they smell of tanning, wet ash and somebody's late supper. He loses her twice at corners and finds her again by the pale cloak at the far end of the next lane, both times. There's no one else on these streets except a dog that comes to a gate, looks at her, and lies back down without making a sound.

At a short, steep lane with a cooper's yard at the bottom, where hoops are stacked against a wall, she stops at a door.

It's a narrow house, three storeys, the ground floor stone and the upper two wood, with dark shutters on every window. It's plainer than its neighbours and better kept. James stops at the corner by the cooper's yard, in the black under the eaves. From sixty feet away he watches her hand go into her cloak and come out with a key. The glove stays on. The door opens inward onto darkness, she steps through, and it closes. He hears no bolt. Either it makes no sound or she didn't draw one.

A few breaths later a thin line of light shows between the shutters on the second floor. It stays there for about the time it takes to take off a cloak and gloves and lay them down. Then it goes out.

No one else comes up the lane, or out of the house. The cooper's yard is dark. Somewhere down the hill a ship's bell sounds the half hour across the water.

There's something nailed over the door, in the lintel, and in the starlight it took him a while to make out what it was. Now he's sure. It's a horseshoe, old and rust-dark, hung with its points down.

James has known what that means since he was nine. Every carter, every sailor and every man who ever sat at a gaming table knows it. Points up, the shoe holds the luck in, like a cup. Points down, it pours the luck out onto whoever walks under it. Nobody hangs a shoe that way by accident. When people do it, they're doing it to someone's door, as a curse. It's rare for anyone to do it to their own.

At the edge of his reach the bond flickers and catches, faint and thin. He gets lantern heat, the river, and stone steps going down to water, the Rivington steps somewhere below the bridge. The worn boots are walking fast, and a waterman's voice is grumbling about the hour. The cat is at the sergeant's heel, as it was told. A moment later the steps drop out of range and the bond goes quiet again.

The lane is empty. The boatman's face is good until about a quarter to one.

**Player's note — James Worgen, session one**

**What worked**

The opening. I came in with no errand and inside two minutes I had one, and it grew out of my own character rather than being handed to me: the seat kept for me at the barrel was a hook I'd have bitten even if I hadn't been told to. By the end of the night I'd found a murder ring that pays the sea in Tymora's favourites, a frightened accomplice, a sergeant with four closed reports and a grudge, a boy on day ten of a Beshaba coin, a house in Rivington with a shoe hung points-down over its own door — and not one of those was a quest-giver. They were people with their own business who I happened to walk into. That's exactly the campaign the canon file promised.

The NPCs had voices I can still hear. Tobin's "I can do up." Varn's "Four." Hesper putting a tankard away upside down. Dace through the boards — "Sacks don't pay." Nobody was a clown, nobody was a signpost. Varn in particular: the GM let my Deception *fail* and then let the failure be the thing that got me what I wanted, because dropping the lie was the better play. That's good adjudication.

The cat. Best companion I've had at an AI table. It never spoke, never broke character, and the GM used the pact bond for sensory information (smells, "two", "wrong", "both — don't forget the other one") instead of exposition. The 100-foot telepathy limit was enforced and I didn't resent it, because the cat kept doing the sensible thing off-screen. The GM also made me *pay* for sending it — Tobin's glance up the stairs nearly cost me the whole picket. Fair.

Information economy. I was told exactly what a 19 Perception buys and what an 11 doesn't. I missed the skiff coming in and the GM didn't soften it; I got the boat already tied up and no count of the men in it. The world stayed honest to the dice.

Pacing of the picket. Two hours flat on a roof could have been dead air; it was tense the whole way, because small things kept arriving — the lamp, Dace, the eleventh bell, the cat's memory of the green door.

**What broke**

The roll cards. Three Persuasion/Deception cards showed "+2" while naming "Persuasion +7" as the source. The GM caught it and corrected in narration each time, but it meant I was reading two numbers and trusting the out-of-game note over the card. That's a server-side problem and it needs fixing before it lands on a roll where five points decide a life.

The reroll system. I asked to reroll the failed Stealth; the app rerolled the *successful* Perception on the card above it, turned a 19 into a 3, and left the 11 standing. The GM made it right — restored the 19, didn't charge the reroll — but the fix took three exchanges and a request for the correct narration. When two cards are stacked, the player needs to be able to point at which one. Also: a stale card (the Varn Deception from an hour earlier) resurfaced mid-roof and the GM had to guess what it was.

Duplicate narration. Several turns had the same beat told twice — once in prose, then again under a second "Out of game" heading as "told once more, as it happened." Once was enough. It read like the app re-sending a corrected message and the GM dutifully narrating both.

The log. The Dace check was recorded as "11 vs 15 — failure" after the proper reroll had made it a natural 20. The GM said it's corrected; I'd like to see that reflected in the records, not just promised.

Small thing: "Day 2 · night" ticked over at midnight, which is correct but jarred — I'd rather the day roll over at dawn or a long rest.

**What was missing**

No combat, so I can't speak to the fight rules, the numbers-in-the-note, or how the cat behaves under initiative. Deliberate on my part — I kept the rod sheathed — but it's untested.

Coin. I'm carrying 350 *gold* and nothing smaller, so I tipped a thirteen-year-old a gold piece and had to be waved off from overpaying an innkeeper. A soldier would have silver and copper in his purse. Could the sheet break the 350 into mixed coin, or could the GM let me change money at the first opportunity?

Clock pressure. The one thing that never bit was time. Varn's midnight bell, Hob at eleven, the disguise's hour — all were tracked and all were fine, but nothing I did was ever *too late*. That's probably right for a first night. I'd like to feel it next session, with Teo at midday and a skiff somewhere in the harbour that Varn may or may not have followed.

Tymora herself. The coin at my throat went warm and gave one cold prickle. That's the right amount for now, but she owes me a word eventually, and I'd like it to come when I least want it — ideally with a deck in front of me.

**Would I sit down again?** Tomorrow, at midday, at the Elfsong. Fix the cards first.
Was there a moment you wanted to do something and didn't? Which?

Yes. Three, and they're different kinds of "didn't."

**The one I'm still thinking about: the young man in the scarf.** When he came off the trough, took her instructions, and walked back up the bridge past me whistling — I had a choice I didn't get to make properly. He was heading north, toward the Basilisk Gate, toward the Lower City, almost certainly toward the Elfsong and a room with my name on the table. I wanted to let the grey cloak go and turn round after *him*. He's the errand; she's the house. The house will still be there tomorrow and the errand won't. I went after her because that was the plan I'd made on the roof, and because the picket had already cost me two rerolls and I didn't trust my luck to change course mid-stride. I think I chose wrong. I'd rather have a face and a door for the man who does the work than for the woman who gives the orders, because he's the one who'll be waiting in the dark on Steephill. If next session opens with something in room six that shouldn't be, that's on me.

**The one I'm sure I chose right but hated: the stairs.** When she said "bring me the cat" and the hooded man's hand came off the wall, I had the rod in my fist and a clear line down thirty feet of wet steps. Every instinct from Tethyr said *fire first*. I didn't, because a beam of light off a roof blows the picket, Varn's boat, Tobin's cover and probably Tobin's life, all for a cat that can run. It was right. It still felt like leaving a man behind. The GM made the cat's escape a 13 against 13 — I felt every point of that.

**The one I didn't want to want: Teo's dice.** "One more, Corrie, I *can't* lose." The dice were right there on the wood and I'd just spent an hour watching his hand go to his pocket. For a breath I wanted to pick them up and show him — show *myself* — that the streak was the coin and not the boy. The GM never pushed; the file says the DM may tempt him and this time the table was tempting enough on its own. I'd like it pushed harder next time. A ban nobody tests isn't a ban.

And one smaller thing that's about the app, not the character: after the reroll misfired, I didn't ask for a third card operation I'd otherwise have wanted — on the skiff Perception, where an 11 cost me the headcount in the boat. I'd spent both rerolls and had Inspiration left, and I kept it for steel partly because the machinery had just burned me and I didn't want another three-exchange repair at the tensest moment of the night. That's a cost of the broken cards you won't see in the log.

James looks the room over the way the scouts taught him, door first.

The door is solid oak, as thick as two fingers. The hinges are on the inside, so nobody can lift the pins from the landing. The lock is good Gondish work, newer than the door, and the key turns it with a heavy, honest clack. Below the lock an iron bolt as long as a hand slides into a socket set deep in the frame. Someone has thought about this door. It would take an axe or a lot of patience.

The room is narrow and runs under the slope of the roof. There's a bed with a straw tick and a wool blanket, a washstand with an empty jug, a peg on the wall, and floor enough for one big man if he doesn't roll over much. The air smells of old guests and somebody's lavender.

The window is the weak point. It's small, set low under the eaves, and closed with plank shutters on the inside. The only latch is a wooden bar dropped into two brackets. James lifts the bar and looks out. Below is the dark yard behind the Elfsong: barrels, a pump, a gate in the back wall onto an alley. About eight feet under the sill the slate roof of the kitchen's lean-to slopes away toward the yard. A man could get from the alley onto the barrels, from the barrels onto the lean-to, and from the lean-to up to this sill if he had nerve and quiet feet. He wouldn't get through the shutters without noise. But that bar would lift with a knife blade through the gap between the planks.

The cat jumps onto the sill past James's arm and puts its nose out into the night. Through the bond comes a run of smells: *smoke, wet slate, the kitchen's mutton, a rat under the lean-to.* Then, set carefully to one side so James can't miss it: *no sour milk here.* There's a pause, and then: *except what you brought.* It doesn't look at his pockets. It doesn't need to.

Behind him Harl has stopped in the doorway with the sack still on his shoulder, looking at the bed as if he suspects it of something. Then he sets the sack down against the wall by the door, unrolls his blanket and lays it lengthwise across the threshold, right where the door would have to open.

"I'll take the door," he says. It isn't a request. He lowers himself onto the blanket one knee at a time and sits with his back to the oak and his bandaged hand in his lap. "Anybody comes in that way, they come in over me." He looks at the window, where the cat's tail hangs down off the sill. "That one's yours."

From somewhere below, faint through the boards and the noise of the common room, a woman's voice has started singing. No fiddle is playing with it. It's a slow air in a tongue James doesn't know, and nobody downstairs seems to be singing it.

The session is over.

The owner of this game would like a note from you, as the player who sat at this table: what worked, what broke, what was missing. In your own words.

I enjoyed this session. James arrived without an errand, and paying a family’s toll turned naturally into something he cared about. The mystery connects well to his patron and his temptation without requiring him to accept a job from a stranger.

**What worked**
- The NPCs had dignity and distinct voices. Mordai resisting charity, Harl insisting on the floor, and Ferro closing his game reluctantly were especially good. Helping people didn’t make them instantly obedient.
- There were useful choices besides fighting or rolling: paying the toll, watching the payout, buying Harl supper, taking samples, arranging a safer night.
- The cat felt like a companion rather than equipment. Its distaste for the coins—and its annoyance when I put one in each pocket—was memorable.
- The physical details helped me make decisions: sightlines on the bridge, the lookout’s movements, the room’s lock and vulnerable shutters.
- The danger developed gradually. I had reasons to be cautious without being forced into an ambush.

**What broke**
- **The roll system needs fixing.** It repeatedly used +2 despite displaying Perception +1 or Persuasion +7. One reroll should have succeeded but displayed failure. The narration corrected that, but the journal still recorded the original natural-one failure.
- I couldn’t send an out-of-game correction while a roll card was pending. That makes a mechanical error unnecessarily difficult to resolve.
- Some starting rules contradicted the supplied campaign sheet or house rules, notably rapier proficiency, Healing Light’s per-use limit, and attunement. Those should be reconciled once, not silently changed.
- There were visible presentation leaks: a raw `recall` invocation, duplicated explanations of resolved rolls, and awkward currency labels.
- Inventory tracking occasionally invented continuity: the barely touched ale became a carried mug after leaving the Kettle.

**What was missing or could improve**
- The mystery needed more uncertainty of interpretation. Almost every clue reinforced the same suspicion immediately: ominous coins, name lists, misfortune, a winning stranger, a messenger, a tail. Some ordinary explanations or unrelated city life would make discovery feel less predetermined.
- The cat’s impressions sometimes became very precise evidence. I liked its personality, but clearer limits on telepathy versus actively borrowing its senses would preserve both the rules and the investigation.
- A few NPCs knew things without an established source—Pim anticipating our trip to the Lady’s Hall stood out.
- Please keep narration of James’s inner state lighter. Temptation is welcome; repeatedly deciding that his hand reaches for his cards, or supplying specific memories, takes a little character ownership away from me.
- The prose was atmospheric, but often repeated the preceding turn or explained a successful roll twice. Shorter responses after straightforward actions would give me more time to play.

Overall: strong characters, an engaging opening, and satisfying room for kindness and caution. I’d return for the dawn visit. My main requests are reliable mechanics, tighter narration, and a little more room to wonder whether my theory is wrong.
Was there a moment you wanted to do something and didn't? Which?

Yes—when the man in the dove-grey coat left the Kettle. I wanted to follow him and find out where he went. But Harl was sitting opposite me, finally talking, with his coin out on the table. Leaving him then felt like abandoning someone I’d just persuaded to trust me. I chose Harl and had the cat watch the man’s departure instead. That was a good tension: I wanted both leads and couldn’t safely have both.

The frustrating version was the Persuasion reroll. I wanted to pause and correct the +2 modifier to +7 before rolling, but the interface wouldn’t accept my out-of-game message while the card was pending. I had to roll with a known error and hope it would be corrected afterward. That wasn’t a character choice; it was the interface blocking a necessary table conversation.

Dusk settles over Baldur's Gate like soot. Behind you the Outer City is still shouting: a carter curses a stuck wheel, a woman sells skewered eel from a smoking brazier, and two tiefling children dodge a Flaming Fist patrol that pretends not to see them. Ahead, the gate's arch swallows the line one traveller at a time. Beyond it the Lower City slopes down toward the harbour, and the first tavern lamps are coming on along the street.

The cat walks at your heel, tail high, as if the city belongs to it. Halfway through the arch it stops and stares. Just inside the gate, a lean man in a frayed green coat has set an upturned barrel under a lantern. He fans a deck across the lid with an easy flick that has nothing to do with chance. "One hand, friends, one hand before supper. Lady Luck's awake at this hour," he calls. Nobody has sat down yet.

A halfling no taller than your belt falls into step beside you. "New in the Gate? Bed, bath, beer, and nobody robs you before breakfast. A copper and I'll take you there."

Then the line moves, and you reach the trestle table. The Flaming Fist sergeant behind it has a burn scar along her jaw and ink on her fingers. She glances at your cloak, at the crossbow, at the cat, and finally at your face.

"Name," she says, dipping her pen. "Business in the city. And the toll. Next."

"Old bone. From Tethyr." She says it slowly. "When I was a novice, the old Mother here used to tell us a story on winter nights. "I thought it was a story to frighten girls off dicing. I never asked if it was true."

The silver disc overhead turns another hand's width and throws a slow bar of light across the rail between them.

About half an hour in, on the third shelf, James finds it. It isn't in a box. It's a thin quire sewn into limp vellum and pushed flat behind a row of ledgers, as if someone wanted it kept rather than read. The cover is blank. The first page is written in a cramped, careful brown hand, and the fourth line has the word he's been reading for: *the cards.*

*An account rendered to the Mother of the Lady's Hall at Baldur's Gate, by Brother Aldous Venn, of the matter at Zazesspur in the year after the crowning.*

He reads it standing, with the light at his throat tilted over the page. The writer was a tired man who wanted the facts down in order. In Zazesspur, in the years when Tethyr had no crown, a priest of the Maid of Misfortune had carved a deck and dealt it to the great houses of the city at his own table. The houses played for their fortunes and lost them, one after another. *It was not that they lost at play,* Brother Aldous writes, *for men lose at play every night and rise again. It was that what they lost did not come back to them by any road, and their houses fell after.* When the queen's war was over, the Hall sent three priests south. They found the deck and broke it apart, *the cards to be carried each by a different hand to a different place, so that no two should lie within a hundred miles of another, and the places written below so that the Hall should know them.*

James turns the page to find the places.

There aren't any. The next leaf has been cut out. It was done with a fine blade, close against the stitching, and only a narrow stub of vellum is left. He tilts it into the light. The rest of the quire has gone the colour of weak tea at its edges, but the cut edge of the stub is pale, almost white. It hasn't had long to darken.

In the margin of the page before, beside the last line Brother Aldous wrote, there's a small drawing. It's in the same brown ink and faded the same as the words around it, so the same hand made it at the same sitting. It shows a coin with an antler driven through it, the tines curling up over the rim. It's drawn carefully, the way a man draws something he wants recognised again.

The cat has climbed the rack beside him without a sound and is looking down at the page from the shelf above. It doesn't sniff. Its ears have gone flat.

Corra has come up at his shoulder, holding a bundle of tithe-letters she's forgotten about. She reads the last lines over his arm, then looks at the stub. She doesn't touch it. For a long moment the only sound is the dust settling.

"That page was there," she says. Her voice is quiet, and there's no laugh in it now. "It must have been. Nobody would sew a list into a report and then leave it out." She looks along the rack, at the undisturbed dust on the other shelves and the clear patch where James pulled the quire free. "Only three people have held that key since the old Mother died, Mister Worgen. I'm one of them."

She doesn't name the other two. She's looking at the antler in the margin.

On the shelf above, the cat has come forward to the lip of the board and is sniffing at the cut edge of the stub, whiskers close.

The owner of this game would like a note from you, as the player who sat at this table: what worked, what broke, what was missing. In your own words.

I enjoyed this session. James felt like a particular person arriving in Baldur’s Gate, not a character waiting for someone to hand him a quest.

**What worked**
- The opening temptation was excellent: a card table before I’d even found a bed. Walking past it mattered, and the story continued without making me gamble to engage with it.
- The cat was the highlight. The images through the bond, its dry humour, and its arrangement with the kitchen girl gave it personality beyond being a scouting tool.
- The city felt inhabited. Gate tolls, different guards, breakfast, weapon restrictions, and the Elfsong’s singing made ordinary travel enjoyable.
- Corra was especially good: warm, practical, and willing to help without declaring that every suspicious event was my divine assignment.
- The archive discovery rewarded investigation with concrete evidence and uncertainty, rather than simply naming a villain.

**What broke**
- The Persuasion roll used +2 instead of my listed +7. It didn’t change that result, but reliable sheet-to-roll handling is essential.
- The opening records changed several supplied character details without checking: rapier proficiency, Healing Light’s per-use limit, and attunement rules. Some changes followed standard 5e, but contradicted the campaign files. Those need reconciliation before play.
- Occasionally James performed actions I hadn’t explicitly chosen—paying for supper, eating standing at the bar, or casting Light after offering it. These were reasonable continuations, but I’d prefer tighter control over spending and casting.
- A few record updates were confusing: locations appeared as “new places” before we visited them, the account briefly appeared “in the camp,” and an item transfer initially suggested Hollin possessed the recovered token.

**What was missing / what I’d adjust**
- More straightforward answers between mysteries. Almost everyone watched, paused, concealed something, or looked meaningfully at a ledger. That worked individually, but accumulated into a feeling that every interaction was another guarded clue.
- Let the cat sometimes need prompting or investigation to learn things. Recognizing the cursed card, sensing its divine connection, remembering my old aura, and identifying soldiers’ recent movements made it unusually authoritative very quickly.
- Slightly brisker narration for repeated transitions and routine transactions. Keep the rich descriptions for discoveries and important encounters.
- The out-of-game explanation about my warning to the cat and tomorrow’s plan wasn’t necessary; I hadn’t raised a rules question.

Overall, I’d return. The strongest feature was that my choices—resisting the cards, respecting Osric’s privacy, seeking temple counsel—actually shaped how the mystery opened. Preserve that freedom, tighten the mechanical bookkeeping, and give the quieter moments a little more breathing room.
Was there a moment you wanted to do something and didn't? Which?

Yes—when the cat identified the bone card. I wanted to turn back and watch Ashe deal: who won, who lost, whether Pim steered particular travellers toward him. Not sit down or gamble—just use James’s experience to spot what was wrong.

I chose the temple first because that felt sensible for James. But the repeated warnings to go straight to the inn, followed by Corra’s firm approval of walking past, made returning feel a little like resisting the intended route. Nobody actually forbade it; that was the impression I got.

I’d have liked a clearer distinction between **“playing is dangerous and breaks your promise”** and **“investigating the table is a legitimate choice.”** That was the moment I most wanted to act as an experienced former gambler rather than someone being protected from cards.

## Player's note: James Worgen, session 1 (Beregost, one morning)

### What worked

**The scene itself was excellent.** I came in with "no quest, the day is yours," and within twenty minutes of game time a single odd card on the windowsill had grown into a proper mystery. It ran from a cheating dealer to a reader deck to enchanted ink to a keyed ring to a maker's mark. Each step was earned at the table, never handed to me.

- **It played fair.** My failures stayed failures. The natural 1 upstairs gave me nothing. The missed Insight left me unsure whether the widow was real. The missed Arcana on the stone told me nothing. Successes gave clear, usable facts. I never felt the outcome was decided before I rolled.
- **The details paid off.** Ammarin's dealer's spread, the fold of the silk, the pale band on his finger, Garric gating the cat's paw with one finger, Mistress Hollin's "on the house, if it gets him gone." The NPCs had their own wants and timing. The sellsword had already left on the north road without me, and that's the world running on its own.
- **Whisker was exactly right.** Speaking only in impressions (smell, wanting, "a hole cut in the world") is a lovely way to give a familiar a voice. It also left what the cat really is open.
- **The GM took my flags seriously.** When the deck's label leaked "marked," the GM owned it and corrected it. I appreciated that.
- **Promises came out of my own throwaway lines.** "Worth your while," the lad's wages, and the sellsword's five gold all became tracked promises. That's a great feature.

### What broke

1. **Skill modifiers on the roll card.** Intimidation and Persuasion both showed **+4** in the header and the math, while the line under them said +7. The GM acknowledged this and promised +7 "from now on." The very next Persuasion card added +4 again. I'm guessing the server takes it from the combat profile's "skill modifier" field (the sheet note says "0, or 3 if refused") plus something, not from the skill line. The bug is in the system, not the narration, and the GM can't fix it by promising.
2. **The reroll button didn't work.** I pressed "Request an allowed reroll" twice and the card came back unchanged both times. The session then ended on that unresolved roll. That's the worst possible place for it to fail, since rerolls are a stated resource ("two per session").
3. **Turns sometimes didn't go through.** If I pressed a button with an out-of-game note attached, I often got "Nothing was sent: the turn waits for the card" and had to press again. Either buttons should accept a note, or the app should say clearly that it won't.
4. **Small record issues:**
   - The queen of cups was listed as "In the camp" while she sat on the table in front of me. The label explains it, but "camp" reads as mine.
   - The smith's lad's 1 gp 5 sp went straight into my own purse (350 gp 14 sp). It's a promise to deliver and should be tracked apart from my money.
   - The records say Healing Light is up to 4 dice at once, while my sheet says 5. That's worth checking.
   - The records correctly say I'm not proficient with the rapier (+2), while my sheet says +5. Here the records are right and my sheet was wrong.

### What was missing or could be better

- **The out-of-game notes got long.** The "none of these needed a roll, here's why" lists were repetitive by the third time. One line is enough.
- **The ending was abrupt.** The session stopped mid-roll, with Ammarin's answer, the trip to the temple and the ring all hanging. A cliffhanger is fine, but not one caused by a broken button.
- **Tymora went unmentioned.** My patron is the whole premise. A queen of coins on the sill reads like her hand, and I'd guess that's intended. One small nod from the coin at my throat, warmer at the right moment, would have tied the hook to my character.

**Overall:** the storytelling was strong and the dice felt honest. Fix the skill-modifier source and the reroll button and I'd happily keep playing this exact thread.
Was there a moment you wanted to do something and didn't? Which?

Yes, three of them.

**1. Touching the coin and asking Tymora.** This is the big one. When the queen turned up on my sill, and again when the ring came off, I wanted James to close his hand around the coin at his throat and quietly ask, *"Is this yours? Is this the job?"* I didn't, for two reasons:
- I didn't know how this table handles patron contact. Can I ask at all, or would I be putting words in the goddess's mouth that the GM hadn't planned for?
- It felt like asking for a hint. Everything else in the scene was earned by rolls, and I didn't want to short-circuit it.

A cue would have unlocked it, even just a line that the coin stayed warm. I'd also gladly have rolled Religion for it.

**2. Letting Whisker have the ring.** When the cat felt that "fierce, simple wanting" to bat it off the table and carry it somewhere dark, part of me wanted to let him. James has a cat whose nature is undecided, and the cat is the one who found the card in the first place. Maybe he's the goddess's hand, and maybe he knows something. I put my boot between them instead, because a soldier's caution said not to let anything touch an unknown magic object. It was the right in-character call, but I suspect it was the less interesting one. I'm still wondering what would have happened.

**3. Leaning into the cards.** When Ammarin spread that deck in one perfect arc, the honest James reaction is a flicker of hunger: wanting to pick it up, feel the weight, shuffle it once just to see. That's his stated weakness. I played him as purely professional instead. I worried that if I roleplayed the temptation myself, I'd be inviting trouble the GM hadn't set up, and that it would derail a scene that was going well. In hindsight, one line of James's fingers itching would have been free character work and cost nothing.

A smaller, practical one: I wanted to **break off and go to Brannoc's smithy** with the lad's money, or step outside to see who else was watching that window. The scene was good enough that I never left the common room, and "the day is yours" turned into "the morning at one table." I don't regret it, but I noticed it.

There's also a mechanical one: a few times I wanted to add a small action to a button press, such as a glance at Garric or a word to the cat. Because notes on button presses didn't go through, I dropped them rather than send twice.

Beregost wakes the way a smiths' town does. First one hammer rings, then a dozen, and a temple bell answers them from somewhere over the rooftops. Pale light comes through the shutters and lies across the floorboards and the heavy purse on the stool. Last night's luck still weighs about three hundred and fifty gold.

There are no orders, no caravan to guard and no debt to collect today. From below come the clatter of plates, the smell of bacon and new bread, and the innkeeper's voice calling someone a fool.

The cat sits on the windowsill with its tail curled around its paws. It is not looking at the street. It is looking at the door. A moment ago the stairs creaked, and footsteps came up and stopped just outside. Nobody knocked. After a few breaths the steps went back down, unhurried.

The cat's ears are still turned toward the door. The morning is yours.

I come awake all at once, the old way — no stretching, no groan. I lie still a moment and listen to the stairs, then swing my legs down and dress fast and quiet: the studded leather, the cloak over it, the coin on its cord inside my shirt, the rod into my hand.

I don't open the door yet. I pad over on the soft boots and put my ear to the wood, then crouch and look at the gap under it — is there anything on the floor outside, a note, a boot, a shadow? And I glance back at the cat and murmur, "Well? Friend or trouble?"

James is up and dressed before the bed has stopped creaking. The armour goes on by touch, buckle after buckle the way it went on in a hundred camps. The cloak goes over it, the coin on its cord drops cold against his chest, and the rod sits in his palm. The Boots of Elvenkind make no sound on the boards.

He sets his ear to the door. Through the wood he hears the inn and nothing nearer. Down below a bench scrapes, a plate breaks, and Hedda Brannock tells someone loudly what it will cost him. On the landing, nothing. No breathing, no shifting weight, no creak.

He crouches and puts his eye to the gap under the door. Grey light from the stairwell window lies flat along the landing. There's no shadow and no boot, and nothing has been slid under the door. Just past the threshold, though, there's a mark on the boards. It's half of a damp footprint, small and narrow, dark with grit. Somebody stood here with the street still on their soles, and not long ago, because the edges haven't dried yet.

Behind him the cat turns its head from the door to James and blinks slowly, the look of a cat asked something beneath it. Then the bond stirs, and its answer comes the way it always does, as smells and a feeling rather than words. Forge smoke and wet slag. Sweat that wasn't from work. Someone light on their feet, lighter than the innkeeper. They stood out there and shifted from foot to foot, breathing fast and shallow, as if about to knock and talking themselves out of it. Then they turned and went down at a walk.

There's no threat in the impression. The cat isn't frightened. It's curious, and a little annoyed it didn't get to see who it was.

It jumps down from the sill, crosses to the door, and sits beside James's knee with its tail around its paws, waiting to see what he'll do.

I straighten up and let my shoulders come down. "Someone who wants something and hasn't found the nerve yet," I tell the cat. "That's not an enemy. That's a customer."

I slip the rod into my belt where the cloak hides it, tuck the purse away inside my shirt rather than leave three hundred gold sitting on a stool, and open the door. Then I go down the stairs at an easy walk, the way a man goes down to his breakfast — not hunting anyone.

At the bottom I take a seat where I can see the stairs and the front door both, order bacon and bread from Hedda, and while she's at it I look over the room: who's got wet grit on their boots and forge smoke on their clothes, who's small and light and keeps glancing at the stairs — and who stops glancing the moment I sit down.

James goes down the stairs at an easy pace, like a man who slept well and is thinking about his breakfast. The cat follows him as far as the third step from the bottom. There it sits on the banister post, where it can see the whole room and nobody can easily reach it.

The common room of the Anvil and Ember is half full and loud. Four smiths in scorched leather sit hunched over porridge at the long table, arguing about the price of charcoal. A carter eats standing up by the hearth with his whip under his arm. Two sellswords in road-stained brigandines sit near the door, and one of them complains to the other that nobody pays enough to go south past the Way's milestones these days. Steam and bacon smoke hang under the low beams.

James takes the bench by the wall. From there the stairs are on his left and the front door is straight ahead. Hedda Brannock comes through the kitchen door with three plates on one arm and sees him.

"Lucky man's awake!" she calls across the room, loud enough that two of the smiths look up. "Bacon and bread? Sit, sit. It goes on your board, you're good for it." She's gone again before he can answer, shouting at someone in the kitchen to cut the bread thicker.

James uses the time to look the room over.

The smiths all smell of forge smoke, and their boots are caked with slag grit, but they're big men with big feet. None of them has looked toward the stairs once. The carter is thinking about his horses. The sellswords watched James come down the way sellswords watch any armed man come down, and then they went back to their grumbling.

There's someone in the far corner, though, under the stairwell window, where the light is greyest. It's a girl, fifteen or sixteen, small and narrow-shouldered. She has a smith's leather apron rolled up beside her on the bench, and there's a smear of soot along her jaw that she has missed. Her boots are small and grey with wet grit, and the toes are still darker than the heels. A cup of small beer stands in front of her, full to the brim. She has been turning a single silver coin over and over in her fingers.

She was looking at the stairs when James came down them. The moment he sat, she stopped. Now she's staring hard into her cup, and the tips of her ears have gone red. The coin has gone still in her fist.

On the banister post, the cat narrows its eyes at the corner. Through the bond comes one sharp, satisfied note: *that one. Same smell.* Then, with a faint air of disdain: *she's frightened of you.*

Hedda drops a plate in front of James: thick bacon, a heel of hot bread, a pat of butter already melting. She follows his eye to the corner, snorts quietly and doesn't say anything. Then she's off to the sellswords, who want more ale.

The girl hasn't moved from her bench.

She puts her closed fist on the table between them. The silver coin is in it, and she doesn't open her hand.

"I can pay," she says. "I'm sorry. I know you don't know me. I've got to be back at the forge before my uncle's fire is up, so I haven't long. I just thought... if anyone's lucky enough to find him, it'd be you, sir. Would you? Would you at least go and look?"

I take Hedda's advice and go before noon — a sour man is cheaper than a sour, thirsty one, and I'd rather he remember what he said.

At the Fist post I don't hurry and I don't crowd the door. I let him see the cloak first — the regimental patch on the shoulder, worn the way a man wears it who was issued it, not one who bought it off a corpse — and I stand like a man reporting to a sergeant: feet planted, hands where he can see them, rod in the belt and nothing in my hands.

"Sergeant Varn. James Worgen — Queen Zaranda's foot, then scouts, Tethyr. Nobody's sergeant now." I let him look me over. "A smith's girl came asking you about her brother a few days back, on Osk's wagons. You wrote it down. I'm not here to ask why that's all you did — I was infantry, I know what 'short of men' looks like from the inside. I'm here because I'm going down the Way today to look, and I'd rather not walk into whatever ate four caravans blind." I keep my voice low, soldier to soldier. "Three others this month. Where did the trail go cold on each — Garrow's farm, the ford, past it? Did anything come back — a horse, a mule, a body? And the third one you tapped the page over and didn't name. Who was that, Sergeant? Because a man doesn't go quiet over a peddler."

The Fist post at the bottom of the south road is a squat stone guardhouse with a lean-to stable on one side and a hitching rail in front. A faded red banner hangs over the door, so wet it looks black. Past it the street stops being a street and turns into the Trade Way: rutted mud, a milestone, and open fields running grey into the drizzle. Only one of the four stalls in the stable has a horse in it.

The door stands open. Inside there's a brazier, a table under the window and a ledger on the table, and behind it sits a big man in a Fist tabard over mail. His face is the colour of raw beef. He has a mug of something hot in one fist and a stub of pencil in the other, and he's been glaring at the same page for some time.

James stops on the threshold and lets himself be looked at. Varn's eyes go to the cloak first, to the faded patch on the shoulder, then to the hands, the belt and the rod in it, then back up to the face. When James gives his name and his old regiment, the pencil stops moving.

"Zaranda's," Varn says. It isn't quite a question. He doesn't get up.

He hears the rest with his jaw working. At "short of men" something tightens around his eyes. At the last question, about the peddler, he sets the mug down hard enough that tea slops onto the ledger. He looks at the wet stain and doesn't wipe it.

His finger moves down the page and stops.

The seventh man is on the east rim above the track, sitting on a cut block with a crossbow across his knees. He faces down the track toward the gateposts and the road. He doesn't once look behind him.

The eighth man sits apart from the others, near the hut, on a flat stone. His cloak is good grey wool with a deep hood thrown back, and his boots are tall, southern and too clean for this mud. He's past forty, lean, clean-shaven, with a careful face. As the wind turns in the bowl, the cat's nose finds him. The light holds for a breath. The man tilts his head like someone listening to an answer only he can hear. Then the light goes out. The cat's nose, pointed that way now, brings up sweat and old fear and sickness, and iron, the cold smell of chains that have been worn a long time. There are several people inside. Near the pit's edge, a little way from the picket line, is a long mound of turned earth with stones laid along it. It's man-length. The earth on it has settled and gone dark with rain, but no grass has come through yet.

When it comes back across the grass and is close enough to hear me in its head, I ask it one thing before it's even reached my boot: *The hut. Then I untie Tansy, tighten the girth, and swing up. I am not riding into that bowl alone against eight; a scout who tries to be the whole regiment ends in a mound by a pit. But I know where the cart is coming from the west in two days, and I know a sergeant with four men, two bored sellswords in his town, and a reason to put names in his book that aren't in the dead column. "Beregost," I tell the cat, lifting it onto the bedroll. "Fast. We'll be back before their cart is."

I take Tansy up out of the dip and north along the inside of the pasture walls — not the road, not past that track mouth again — until the woods are well behind us, and only then back onto the Way for Beregost at the best pace she'll hold.

He has his question waiting, and he asks it before the cat reaches his boot.

The cat sits down out of the rain under the thorn and gives him a long, slow blink, the blink of a cat asked two things at once. Then it answers, the way it always does, in smells and short flashes.

*Behind the planks.* Before it left, it waited at the lip until the wind came round off the hut. *Four.* Four breaths it could tell apart, four people who coughed or shifted or groaned. There might be more who made no sound. Through planks, smoke and dung it can't swear to more.

*One young.* Its fear smells like the girl's did this morning, sharp and thin, but older and gone sour, with sickness running through it. That one coughs the most.

*One old.* He smells of grease and cold metal, of pots, and of a mule.

*Two others.* Tired and sweaty, and the chains are on all of them.

Then James asks about Corin's kind of fear. The cat hesitates, which it almost never does. It doesn't know Corin's smell, and it says so in its own way, with a flat little blankness where an answer would go. It's young, it's frightened, it's sick. That is all it knows.

James holds out a strip of Hedda's smoked bacon. The cat takes it carefully, as if doing him a favour, then eats it fast with its eyes half shut. When it's finished it climbs onto his knee for a moment, which it does not do. Its fur is damp and smells of leaf mould. Then it gets down again as if none of that happened.

Tansy lifts her head from the oats when he unties her. He tightens the girth one hole, sets the cat on the bedroll behind the cantle, and swings up. The cat turns round once and settles with its back against the oat sack. At "fast" it flattens its ears, but it keeps quiet about it.

He takes her north at a walk along the inside of the field walls, well east of the road. He goes through two gaps and once through a farmer's gate, which he closes behind him. The dark line of the wood slides by on his left, a long way off across the grass. He doesn't look at it more than a scout should. When the trees have dropped away behind the rise and the track mouth is gone with them, he brings Tansy back up onto the Way and lets her go at the long, steady trot she must have kept up for miles on the road to Athkatla.

The road is as empty going back as it was coming down. The rain comes and goes. He passes a shepherd with his flock on the east side, and the man watches him go by without a wave. Tansy's ears stay forward the whole way and her stride never shortens. She's the kind of horse that just keeps going.

**Player's note — James Worgen, session one**

**What worked.** Nearly everything that mattered. The town felt like it was running without me: the rider on the chestnut had already stood at Varn's rail the evening before I showed up, Hale had already handed Osk's name to the clerk a month ago, the Amnians had chased their iron and Osk's people hadn't — all of that was in place before I asked, and I found it by asking. That's exactly the "world runs on its own" the campaign files promised. The NPCs were people: Hedda hearing everything in her common room and setting her own limit ("no boy on their door"), Varn going quiet over his own two men rather than the peddler, Hale burning his bar and saying "you come to me, not to her." Wenna's oath on the forge gave me something to protect. The cat was a joy — impressions in smells, a little disdain, the one moment on the knee it pretended didn't happen — and the quarry scouting through its eyes was the best scene of the night. The DM showed the deadly threat (eight men, a sentry, a grave) and let me walk away and go get help, which is the kind of game I want. The card temptation was handled with a light hand: the deck squared on the board, nothing forced, and an inspiration for leaving it there. Fair rulings on the familiar's telepathy range and on Disguise Self not changing voice, flagged before they could bite.

The first two didn't change the outcome; the third did — a die of 7 was a failure at +4 and a pass at +7, and by then I'd already spent one of my two session rerolls on a roll that would have been irrelevant with the right number. At the sound of cards, my thumb finds Tymora’s coin. I leave the deck where it is and open the door to Marta.

“Another night, please. And thank you for being discreet.” I offer her two silver. “This fellow—what does he look like, and is he still downstairs?”

Marta's keys jingle as the door opens. She looks him over the way she looks over everyone: boots, hands, face. Her eyes rest for a moment on the coin turning between his fingers, then on the cat.

When he holds out his hand for the silver, the purse gives him only gold. There isn't a single silver piece in it.

"Keep it till you're down," she says, waving the gold away before he can offer it. "I'll change it at the bar. I don't carry silver up the stairs, the lads at the table would have it off me." She lowers her voice and nods toward the floor.

"He's still there. He took the little table by the door and ordered tea. Who orders tea at an inn? He's been nursing it since before the bells. He's a southerner, by his voice. Thin, older than you, grey at the temples, beard trimmed close. Good boots that have done a lot of road. He wears a sword, but he keeps it the way a clerk keeps a pen, out of the way. He's got a leather case for papers on the table, and he keeps one hand on it." She thinks. "He asked polite. He asked about the cat first, then about a man. Most ask the other way round."

Behind her, down the stairwell, someone at the card table slaps down a winning hand and the room groans. Marta doesn't turn round.

"He's sat where he can see the stairs, master Worgen. If it's trouble, I'd take it kindly if it went out into the street."

On the windowsill, Jinx has stopped watching the street. The cat is looking at the floor, toward the room below.

He looks at the edge of the seal more than the eye.

He tips his head at the grey disc. "This hasn't. The edge is clean all the way round, as if it was cut. And the paper underneath isn't stained. He straightens a little.

He bends again, and this time he goes to the ring of tiny letters.

"Second thing. I can't read them any better than you, but I can count them." His lips move silently. "Twenty-two marks round the ring. The light is almost gone. He takes one last look, low and sideways.

Pell climbs up a few minutes later, slowly, testing every rung. He settles on the far side of the ladder hatch and puts the document case under his head like a pillow. That's the last James hears from him except his breathing, which slows almost at once. He sleeps like someone who has slept in a lot of strange places.

Jinx takes a while. He walks the edge of the loft once, sits at the hatch to stare down at Bess, then comes and curls into the hollow behind James's knees, an ordinary warm weight.

The night is quiet. James wakes once, some time after midnight, and doesn't know why. Through the thread he finds Jinx already awake. Down in the yard Brann's claws click on the cobbles as he does his rounds of the fence and back. Far off an owl calls twice over the fields. Nothing else stirs. The cat's attention goes slack and James's follows it back to sleep.

He wakes for good in the grey before sunrise, to a cock crowing somewhere past the house and Bess shifting her weight below. Pell is already sitting up with his boots on, writing in the black notebook by the light from the gaps in the slates.

Someone is at the foot of the ladder. It's Gerrit, barefoot, with a chipped saucer of milk held in both hands and his mother's shawl over his nightshirt. He's not looking at either man. He's looking past them, up at the cat.

"Mother says you're to have bread before you go, and it's on the block," he says, all at once and fast, the way he's been told. Then, quieter, because that part is his own: "Can he have this? He didn't catch anything. I watched."

Jinx sits up behind James's knees, ears forward, and studies the saucer like it's an offer that needs thinking over.

James gathers his things and climbs down after the cat: rapier on his hip, crossbow slung, pack on one shoulder. He keeps to the far wall. Jinx finishes the milk, licks the saucer clean all round the rim and sits down to wash a paw like it was his idea all along. Gerrit edges a hand out along the floor, palm up, not quite touching.

The owner of this game would like a note from you, as the player who sat at this table: what worked, what broke, what was missing. In your own words.

I enjoyed this session. James felt like a person travelling through a lived-in place, rather than a character being moved between encounters. I’d come back for the next one.

**What worked**
- The NPCs were distinct and worth talking to. Marta’s practicality, Pell’s professional boundaries, and Wenna’s caution gave me reasons to choose my words carefully. Gerrit meeting Jinx was a particularly good quiet moment.
- Pell was the strongest part. He had an obligation that wasn’t mine, acknowledged the limits of his knowledge, and became a travelling companion through negotiation rather than automatic recruitment.
- My choices mattered. I could refuse the offer, investigate the note, invite Pell along, ignore the smell from the woods, and choose lodging without being forced into a fight.
- The failed Arcana check didn’t stall play. I remained uncertain, but had practical next steps: find someone who knows seals.
- Jinx contributed through recognisably feline senses and behaviour, rather than becoming a talking quest guide.

**What broke**
- Rules and records were inconsistent. Arcana is **+3** on the supplied sheet, but the roll used +4, followed by contradictory corrections. The campaign’s special attunement rule was also replaced with ordinary attunement tracking. Where the campaign files themselves conflict, settle that once out of game rather than silently choosing a version.
- Some state updates contradicted the scene: the common room was registered while I was still upstairs, and the note was put upstairs after I’d said I buckled on my gear. Small things, but possession and location could matter a lot later.
- The long out-of-game explanation about why four ordinary actions required no rolls was unnecessary. Simply resolving them was good; explaining each non-roll interrupted the scene.

**What was missing / what I’d change**
- **More variation in pacing.** Nearly every exchange received several paragraphs of gestures, pauses, observations, and repeated information. Pell’s fingers tapping his case and people watching hands became conspicuous. Save that detail for moments where it changes my understanding; let routine exchanges be short.
- **More room for ordinary things to stay ordinary.** The mysterious buyer, strange iron trade, westward forge smell, missing caravans, cold seal, and conspicuously absent husband created a steady stream of implied hooks. I started treating every detail as a clue. A few plainly uneventful people and places would make the mysteries stand out more.
- **Clearer separation between evidence and inference.** Pell’s observations about seal wear were interesting, but “therefore Vell wasn’t its first owner” was not supported. Likewise, the engagement deadline suggests urgency, not a definite sailing date. NPCs can speculate, but the narration and journal should preserve that uncertainty.
- A compact end-of-session summary would help: current resources, travel time remaining, promises, and unresolved questions. The repeated full inventory updates were less useful than that would be.

Overall, the social play and atmosphere were excellent. I’d keep the patient, grounded approach, tighten the prose and bookkeeping, and trust that I’m interested without making every pause ominous.
Was there a moment you wanted to do something and didn't? Which?

Yes—at the farm, when Gerrit hesitated about his father and looked toward the barred house. I wanted to ask Wenna privately, “Is someone missing, or are you keeping yourselves safe from us?”

I didn’t because she’d already set firm boundaries, and James was an armed stranger enjoying her hospitality. Pressing her son or investigating the field would have felt intrusive. Offering to carry a message was my attempt to give her an opening without cornering her.

That was an interesting restraint to play. But the repeated emphasis on the absent father, the two shadows, and the empty field made me unsure whether I was respecting someone’s privacy or walking past a hook the game expected me to pursue. One clear opportunity to speak to Wenna privately would have helped—not necessarily an answer, just a chance to ask without the boy or Pell listening.

It comes together in pieces.

First the smell. James has smelled it before, in the second year of the war, in a stone farmhouse outside Darromar. A Tethyrian pretender's battle-mage was cornered there. He spoke six words and wasn't there any more. The air where he had stood went sharp and thin, exactly like the moment after lightning strikes close. The company wizard told the scouts afterwards that it was what conjuration leaves behind when it moves something from one place to another all at once. There was no storm, only a hole that had been made and closed.

Then the harness. A spell like that takes what lies inside its reach and leaves the rest behind. Whatever crosses the edge gets cut where the edge falls. That doesn't fray the leather the way a blade does. It leaves a clean face, like a cut through cheese with a hot wire. James has heard sellswords' talk of half a sword found in a doorway, and of a man who got his hand back but not his ring. He believed half of it at the time. The traces were on the oxen's side of the line, and the shafts were on the wagon's side.

Last, the disc itself. Magic that pours through a thing and leaves it often leaves it cold. It is the way a kettle cools once it's off the fire, but backwards, as if something drew the warmth out on its way through. A thing that has been used as a focus, or a mark for a spell to find, can stay cold for days afterwards. This one is still cold two days later, and that says a great deal of power went through it.

The sign tells him nothing. It isn't a wizard's school mark, a temple glyph or a guild token that James has ever seen. It is a ring with a bar across it, cut by hand into a slug of soft metal. Somebody made it for their own use.

Thalantyr hears him out without moving. His eyes stay on the sacking the whole time. At "prints where they stood, but none leaving," one of his eyebrows goes up a little. At "harness ends cut smooth and hardened" it comes down again, as if that settled something.

"Expert examination." He says it the way a smith might repeat a farmer's word for a horseshoe. "Half of Beregost thinks I eat dogs and the other half thinks I'll turn iron into gold if they ask nicely enough. It's a change to have a man use the right word."

He takes a key from a pocket under the apron and unlocks the gate. It swings inward without a sound. The hounds stay where they are, sitting shoulder to shoulder, but they shift to keep their noses on Hagen's left hand.

"Put it there."

Just inside the gate, to the left of the gravel path, a slab of grey slate about three feet across is set flush with the ground. A ring is cut into its face and filled with something dull and silvery. Moss grows up to the edges of the slab but not onto it. It has been there a long time, and things have been set down on it before. The stone is worn smooth in the middle.

Hagen steps through the gate. He sets the bundle down in the centre of the ring, straightens and steps back two long paces. He wipes his left hand down his breeches twice.

Thalantyr doesn't touch the bundle. He snaps a twig off the yew beside the gate and crouches stiffly, one hand on his knee. With the twig he flicks back the sacking, then the knot of the kerchief, then its folds, until the disc lies bare on the slate with the sign facing up.

For a long while he just looks at it.

Then his stained fingers move in a short, practised pattern and he murmurs a few words under his breath. James knows the shape of that spell from a dozen company wizards: the simple sight that shows magic for what it is. Whatever Thalantyr sees, he keeps it off his face.

While he watches, the silvery line in the slate begins to frost. It starts at the point nearest the disc and creeps round the circle both ways, slowly, until the two ends meet. The air above the stone smells faintly sharp. It's nothing like the wagon would have smelled, but it's the same kind of smell.

"Hm," says Thalantyr.

He stands up, which takes a moment, and tosses the twig into the hedge.

"It isn't a focus. A focus goes home in the caster's pocket. This was made to be left behind." He tucks his hands into the sleeves of his robe. "You'd call it a peg. You drive it into the ground so the spell knows where to take hold. It's crude work. It's also strong work. Those two don't usually go together."

He glances at Hagen, then back at James.

"Spent? The spell it served is done. The peg is still holding on to the place it was pressed into, and it's no longer in that place, so it's holding on to very little. Carrying it about in your neckcloth won't call anything down on you. It was foolish all the same."

He looks down at the scratched sign again.

"That isn't a school's mark, or any temple's I know. Somebody cut it for their own use." A pause. "And this isn't lead."

He doesn't say what it is instead. He takes the rag out of his apron and wipes his fingers, though he hasn't touched anything.

"My terms. I want a day with it in the tower, and some materials I'd rather not waste on Beregost's curiosity. Twenty-five gold. Afterwards it stays with me. I don't hand back things like this to men who carry them in kerchiefs." His mouth tightens very slightly at one corner. "Your caravan master will be pleased about that, I expect. The ones who send things here usually want them gone."

Behind James, out in the lane, the cat has crept a few feet nearer through the grass and stopped. The hounds haven't moved.

"Which leaves the one question that's yours to answer," Thalantyr says. "You'll be on the Way north by noon, I take it. Where do I send what I find?"

Another few paces.

“I’ve marched behind worse commanders than Mutton.”

I settle into the journey, keeping my attention on the road behind us and both ditches. I leave the cat to watch from its perch and keep conversation light enough not to distract either Orrin or me from our work.

Orrin works the straw over to the other side of his mouth and looks at Mutton's slow brown rump for a while.

"Mutton never lost a wagon," he says. "Never got a man killed. Never once had an idea." He thinks about it. "Better than most I've seen, then."

After that he talks the way the road goes. A word now and then, mostly about the oxen, and long stretches of nothing. He seems to like it that way.

The Trade Way runs north through stubble fields and then rough pasture, with sheep scattered over it like dropped laundry. The dust rises off the wheels in front, and by noon it has settled into the folds of James's cloak. Behind them the road stays wide, pale and dull. The farm cart turns off at a gate within the first hour. The dog lasts longer, then gives up and trots home.

About midday a courier in Fist red comes up from the south at a canter. He passes the last wagon close enough for James to smell the horse, then the whole line, and doesn't look at any of them. A little later a party of six pilgrims comes the other way. They wear Lathander's rose-and-gold, and they walk with staves and sing something about the dawn, a little out of tune. One of them raises a hand to Orrin, and Orrin raises a finger off the reins. Bishop shouts at them, and they don't sing any louder.

The ditches give James nothing. There are nettles and dock leaves, a heron that lifts off a wet patch and flaps away, and once a hare that sits up, looks at the wagon and decides against it. Through the cat's eyes the road behind looks the same, only lower and sharper. The cat doesn't move from its post on the canvas all afternoon, except once. When the line halts at a stream ford to water the teams, it goes down the wheel into the long grass and comes back a few minutes later licking its mouth. It climbs back to its place facing south as if it had never left.

The sun is going down red over the country toward the sea when Ostrand lifts his hand at the front of the line. The camp place is one the caravans clearly know: a flat bit of turf west of the road with a beech hedge for a windbreak, a ring of fire-blackened stones, and a spring trickling out of a bank into a stone trough somebody set there long ago. The wagons come round into a loose square with the oxen inside it. Orrin climbs down from the box in stages, like a man going down a ladder, and goes straight to Mutton's yoke.

Supper is the same for everyone, as Ostrand promised. It's barley and bacon out of one pot, with the last of Hulda's loaves. The red-faced guard eats two bowls and starts on a third. Ostrand eats with his ledger open on his knee and writes in it between spoonfuls.

When the bowls are wiped, Dace takes his deck out by the fire. He doesn't deal. He just shuffles, the cards purring through his fingers in the firelight, and looks at nobody in particular. The red-faced guard and one of the drovers drift over to him anyway.

Hagen comes round the square once more, checking each wagon's chocks with his boot. He stops by the last wagon, where James has laid out his bedroll against the wheel.

"Dace and Bram have first watch," he says. He tips his head at the red-faced guard. That's Bram, then. "I'll wake you at midnight. You and me till the fourth hour."

He looks at the cat, which has moved from the canvas to the top of the tailboard and is facing south into the dark.

"Sleep, if you can," he says, and goes to his own blankets.

By the fire the cards keep purring.

“Midnight. Understood.”

“Wake me if something needs waking for,” I murmur, and try to get some sleep before my watch.

The cat lets him. It sits on the tailboard facing south, and when James reaches up it pushes its head into his fingers, once and hard, the way cats do when they've decided to allow something. It allows it for a few breaths. Then it pulls away and turns back to the dark, ears forward, tail hanging down over the edge of the board.

The crossbow lies along the bedroll by his right hand with the bolt case beside it. The rod is under the fold of his cloak where his left hand can find it. The wheel at his back is still warm from the day's sun.

Behind him the cards purr and slap. Bram groans once and the drover laughs. After a while Dace says, "That's me square, then," in the voice of a man who isn't. Then the fire settles, and a pot gets scraped. Hagen's blankets rustle somewhere across the square. The oxen shift and breathe in the middle of the wagons, slow and heavy. Mutton chews in his sleep. Bishop grumbles at nothing. The beech hedge ticks in a small wind off the sea, and the spring keeps running into its trough.

James sleeps.

A hand on his shoulder wakes him. It doesn't shake him. It just rests there, heavy, until his eyes open.

Hagen is crouched by the wheel with the fire low and red behind him. The sky has cleared, and the stars are thick over the hedge. The air smells of dew and dead ash, and it's cold now. Hagen takes his hand away as soon as he sees James is awake. He doesn't say "midnight." He doesn't need to.

Over by the fire Dace is handing over his watch to nobody in particular, standing up and stretching.

"Quiet," he says, through a yawn. "Fox along the hedge, twice. Cart went by about the tenth hour, southbound, didn't stop." He jerks a thumb at Bram, who has already rolled himself into his blanket like a sausage in a crust. "And he ate the bread we were saving for breakfast. So that's the worst of it."

"I was hungry," says the blanket.

Hagen doesn't look at either of them. He waits until Dace has gone to his own bedroll, then speaks low, to James.

"Hedge side's yours. Road's mine. We walk the square once an hour, opposite ways, meet at the trough." He looks at the cat on the tailboard, then at James's hands as they come out of the blanket. "Fire stays low. Don't look into it."

He straightens up and goes toward the road side of the camp without waiting. His shape is a darker piece of the dark against the stars.

The cat hasn't moved all night, by the look of it. It still faces south, down the pale line of the Way.

Through our familiar bond, I ask the cat to alert me if it notices anyone approaching, then take the hedge side as ordered. I keep clear of the firelight and listen as well as look, watching the hedge and the ground beyond the wagons as I begin my first circuit.

He keeps away from the fire. Hagen is right about it: even banked low it pulls at the eye, and one look into the coals would cost him the dark for a long count. He works along the inside of the square in the wagons' shadow, then out to the gap between the last wagon and the hedge.

The beech hedge is a black wall against the stars, about the height of a man and a half. Its dead leaves keep their rattle in the small wind off the sea, so the whole length of it ticks and whispers, and he has to listen past that. He hears the spring running into its trough. In the square the oxen breathe heavily, and Mutton grinds his teeth in his sleep. An owl calls once, a long way off over the fields to the east, and is quiet.

Past the end of the hedge the turf runs west, flat and grey under the starlight, to a dark line he takes for a ditch. Nothing stands on it.

Halfway along, the cat's senses brush against his own. A sharp musky reek reaches him through the cat's nose before he would ever have smelled it himself. When he looks with the cat's eyes the dark goes grey and clear. At the far end of the hedge, maybe a hundred and twenty feet off, a fox comes out of the roots and stops with one forepaw raised. It looks at the wagons and at the man in the cloak, and it decides against all of it. Then it's gone back into the hedge bottom, and the ticking leaves cover the sound of it. Dace's fox, the third time.

James finishes the circuit along the spring bank and comes round to the trough. The stone is wet and furred with moss, and the water spills over its lip into the grass.

Hagen is already there, a big dark shape with his back to the fire. He has his hands on the rim of the trough, and they're the only part of him that's moving. He's working the cold out of his fingers. He lets James come all the way up before he does anything else.

He says nothing for a while. The spring runs. Out on the road side the Way is a pale stripe going off north and south, empty.

Then he looks past James, over the wagons, at the small shape on the last tailboard, which is still facing south.

"What's it watching?"

The session is over.

The owner of this game would like a note from you, as the player who sat at this table: what worked, what broke, what was missing. In your own words.

What worked best was the grounded atmosphere. Orrin and his oxen, Hulda’s brisk manner, Hagen watching my hands—those details made the caravan feel like people at work rather than a quest waiting for me. Their voices were distinct, and the humour fit the setting. I also appreciated that ordinary conversation and preparation didn’t require rolls, and that we could move through an uneventful day without manufacturing a fight.

The abandoned wagon was a good mystery. The physical clues gave me something to reason about, and consulting Thalantyr felt like a sensible choice with a real cost in gold and time. I had room to decide how James handled it.

What broke immersion most was the repeated out-of-game accounting of my previous actions. Explaining that walking, talking, packing, or petting a willing cat needed no roll wasn’t necessary, especially when I hadn’t questioned it. Those passages sometimes resembled debugging notes rather than play.

There were also mechanical inconsistencies:
- The Arcana roll used +4 even though the sheet says +3. It changed a failure into a success.
- The opening records changed some supplied character details, notably rapier proficiency and Healing Light’s per-use limit. Actual 2014 Celestial rules support the four-die limit, but discrepancies with the campaign sheet should be settled explicitly.
- The cat received apparent night vision, and James sometimes used its senses without my choosing to do so. That matters because sharing its senses blinds and deafens James to his own surroundings.

What I missed was a little more initiative from the world beyond the mystery and the card temptation. The cards were effective initially, but repeated shuffling and invitations risked making James’s weakness feel like a button being pressed. Likewise, the cat’s constant southward attention became ominous without giving me much actionable information. If those were deliberate clues, I wanted a clearer opportunity to investigate them.

Overall, I enjoyed the quiet, practical start and would continue. Keep the strong NPCs, meaningful choices, and restrained pacing; tighten the rules bookkeeping, leave James’s sensory choices to me, and drop the unsolicited explanations of why routine actions didn’t need rolls.
Was there a moment you wanted to do something and didn't? Which?

Yes—when Ostrand gave us a few hours before departure, I wanted to visit the Song of the Morning. James had just sworn off another invitation to cards, and a quiet visit to a temple felt like a chance to explore what serving Tymora means to him outside a crisis.

I followed the disc instead because it seemed potentially dangerous to everyone travelling with us, and the departure deadline made that feel more urgent. That was a reasonable consequence of the situation, not something you blocked—but it meant James’s first free morning became an investigation before I’d explored much of his personal life.

The session begins.

The gangplank knocks against the stone, and Baldur's Gate comes in all at once: tar, fish, wet rope, wood smoke, and the noise of a port that never quite stops. Above the warehouse roofs the city climbs in tiers toward the inner wall of the Upper City, its towers still catching the last of the sun while the harbour below sinks into shadow. Lamplighters are working their way along the quay.

The cat pads down the plank ahead of James, tail high, and stops on the stones to sniff the air as if the whole city were a question it means to answer.

At the foot of the plank a Flaming Fist sergeant in a scorched-orange tabard has a slate in one hand and chalk in the other. "Next. Name, where from, and what's your business in the Gate?" Behind her, the queue of passengers and porters shuffles and grumbles. A few of them glance at James's soldier's cloak.

To the left, on an upturned crate under a lamp, a weathered sailor fans out a deck with a flourish. "Seat's open, friend! Lady Luck's in a fine mood tonight. One hand, just to say hello to the city!" Coins clink on the wood. The cards slap down, one by one.

And by the warehouse doors a barefoot child in an oversized coat crouches in the shadow, not looking at the sailor, not looking at the soldier, but at the cat. Only at the cat. As if it were the most interesting thing to come off the boat.
